CBAP Cheat Sheet — KA1: Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring

Exam Weight: ~16% of exam questions. This KA is foundational — its outputs (the various "approaches") serve as guidelines/tools for ALL other KAs. Expect roughly 19 scenario-based questions directly testing KA1 concepts.

1. PURPOSE OF THIS KA

This KA defines how the BA organizes and coordinates their own BA work. It is NOT about project planning — it's about planning the analysis effort itself.

Critical exam distinction:

  • Project Plan = PM's responsibility (scope, schedule, budget)
  • BA Plan/Approach = BA's responsibility (how to elicit, analyze, manage requirements)

2. THE 5 TASKS — Quick Reference

#TaskPrimary OutputCore Question
1Plan Business Analysis ApproachBusiness Analysis ApproachHow will we do BA work?
2Plan Stakeholder EngagementStakeholder Engagement ApproachWho do we work with and how?
3Plan Business Analysis GovernanceGovernance ApproachWho decides and how?
4Plan Business Analysis Information ManagementInformation Management ApproachHow do we organize BA info?
5Identify Business Analysis Performance ImprovementsBA Performance AssessmentHow well are we doing BA?

3. TASK-BY-TASK DEEP DIVE

TASK 1: Plan Business Analysis Approach

Purpose: Decide the overall methodology and level of formality for BA work.

Inputs:

  • Needs (external — from Strategy Analysis or sponsor)

Output:

  • Business Analysis Approach

Key Elements:

  • Predictive vs. Adaptive: The BA must align with the organization's methodology
  • Predictive (plan-driven): Requirements defined upfront, formal sign-offs, detailed documentation
  • Adaptive (change-driven): Requirements evolve, iterative elaboration, lightweight documentation
  • Hybrid: Mix of both — increasingly common
  • Timing of BA activities: When will analysis happen relative to other project phases?
  • Complexity and risk: Higher risk/complexity → more formal approach
  • Deliverables and level of formality: What documentation, what format?

Techniques Used:

  • Brainstorming
  • Business Cases
  • Document Analysis
  • Estimation
  • Financial Analysis
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Modelling
  • Reviews
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Scope Modelling
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • "BA approach" ≠ "BA plan." The approach is the methodology/strategy; the plan is the collection of all planning outputs together.
  • If a question asks what the BA does FIRST on a new initiative → Plan BA Approach (before stakeholder engagement, before governance).
  • Don't confuse this with project methodology selection — BA doesn't choose Agile vs. Waterfall for the project; they align their BA approach WITH whatever methodology is already in use.

TASK 2: Plan Stakeholder Engagement

Purpose: Identify stakeholders, analyze their characteristics, and define how the BA will collaborate with them.

Inputs:

  • Needs (external)
  • Business Analysis Approach (from Task 1)

Output:

  • Stakeholder Engagement Approach

Key Elements:

  • Stakeholder identification: Who has a stake in the change?
  • Stakeholder analysis: Authority, influence, attitude (positive/negative/neutral)
  • Stakeholder roles: Domain SME, end user, sponsor, regulator, tester, implementation SME, project manager, supplier
  • Communication needs: What does each stakeholder need to know, when, and how?
  • Collaboration planning: How will you work with each group?

Stakeholder Analysis Dimensions (memorize these):

DimensionDescription
AuthorityPower to make decisions
InfluenceAbility to affect others' decisions
AttitudeSupportive, resistant, or neutral toward the change
InterestLevel of concern about the outcome
Complexity of needsHow elaborate their requirements are

Techniques Used:

  • Brainstorming
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Scope Modelling
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas ← primary technique
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Stakeholder engagement ≠ stakeholder analysis. Engagement is the TASK (planning how to work with them). Analysis is a TECHNIQUE used within that task.
  • A question about "identifying who should approve requirements" is NOT stakeholder engagement — it's governance (Task 3).
  • "The BA discovers a new stakeholder mid-project" → This means the Stakeholder Engagement Approach needs to be UPDATED (planning is iterative, not one-time).
  • Stakeholders include people OUTSIDE the project team: regulators, customers, suppliers.

TASK 3: Plan Business Analysis Governance

Purpose: Define how decisions about requirements and designs will be made, who has authority, and how changes are controlled.

Inputs:

  • Business Analysis Approach (from Task 1)
  • Stakeholder Engagement Approach (from Task 2)

Output:

  • Governance Approach

Key Elements:

  • Decision making: Who approves requirements? What is the escalation path?
  • Change control process: How are changes to requirements handled?
  • Prioritization approach: How will requirements be ranked?
  • Approval process: What constitutes sign-off? Who signs off?
  • Conflict resolution: What happens when stakeholders disagree?

Techniques Used:

  • Brainstorming
  • Document Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Modelling
  • Reviews
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Governance is about DECISION AUTHORITY, not about managing documents (that's Task 4).
  • "Two stakeholders disagree on priority" → The answer involves the governance approach, NOT stakeholder engagement.
  • "Who should approve the final requirements?" → Governance question.
  • Don't confuse BA governance with organizational governance or IT governance — BA governance specifically covers requirements-related decisions.

TASK 4: Plan Business Analysis Information Management

Purpose: Define how BA information (requirements, models, designs) will be stored, accessed, and reused.

Inputs:

  • Business Analysis Approach (from Task 1)
  • Governance Approach (from Task 3)

Output:

  • Information Management Approach

Key Elements:

  • Organization of BA information: Structure, categorization, hierarchy
  • Level of abstraction: How detailed? Business vs. technical requirements?
  • Traceability approach: How will you track relationships between requirements?
  • Forward traceability: Requirement → Design → Implementation
  • Backward traceability: Implementation → Design → Requirement → Need
  • Reuse of requirements: Can existing requirements be leveraged?
  • Storage and access: Tools, repositories, version control
  • Requirements attributes: Status, priority, source, owner, complexity, stability

Traceability Relationship Types (heavily tested):

RelationshipMeaning
DeriveRequirement B is derived from Requirement A
DependRequirement B depends on Requirement A
SatisfySolution component satisfies a requirement
CoverTest case covers a requirement

Techniques Used:

  • Brainstorming
  • Document Analysis
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Process Modelling
  • Reviews
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Traceability questions are VERY common. Know the 4 relationship types above.
  • "Where should the BA store approved requirements?" → Information Management, NOT governance.
  • "The BA needs to know if a change to one requirement affects others" → This is a TRACEABILITY question (Information Management).
  • Requirements attributes (status, priority, source, etc.) are defined here, NOT in Requirements Life Cycle Management.

TASK 5: Identify Business Analysis Performance Improvements

Purpose: Assess the BA's own performance and identify ways to improve BA processes.

Inputs:

  • Business Analysis Approach (from Task 1)
  • Business Analysis Performance Assessment (self-referencing — previous assessments)

Output:

  • Business Analysis Performance Assessment

Key Elements:

  • Performance analysis: Are BA activities meeting their objectives?
  • Measures: Accuracy of estimates, frequency of rework, stakeholder satisfaction, defect rates in requirements
  • Root cause analysis: Why are problems occurring in BA work?
  • Preventive actions: How to avoid future issues?
  • Improvement recommendations: What should change in the BA approach?

Techniques Used:

  • Brainstorming
  • Document Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Metrics and KPIs
  • Observation
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Reviews
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • This is the ONLY task that explicitly monitors BA performance itself.
  • This task is ONGOING — not just at project end. Performance can be assessed at any time.
  • "The BA notices that elicitation sessions consistently run over time" → Performance Improvement task.
  • "Requirements defects found in testing are increasing" → Performance Improvement task (the BA assesses their own process).
  • Don't confuse this with Solution Evaluation — that KA evaluates the solution, not the BA process.

4. INPUTS AND OUTPUTS — MASTER MAP


Needs (external)
    │
    ├──→ Plan BA Approach ──→ Business Analysis Approach
    │         │
    │         ├──→ Plan Stakeholder Engagement ──→ Stakeholder Engagement Approach
    │         │         │
    │         │         └──→ Plan BA Governance ──→ Governance Approach
    │         │                   │
    │         │                   └──→ Plan BA Info Management ──→ Info Management Approach
    │         │
    │         └──→ Identify BA Performance Improvements ──→ BA Performance Assessment
    │                     ↑                                        │
    │                     └────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │                              (self-referencing loop)

Key insight for exam: The outputs flow INTO the other 5 knowledge areas as guidelines and tools. This is why KA1 is foundational.

5. TECHNIQUES MAPPED TO TASKS

Memory tricks:

  • Universal techniques (all 5 tasks): Brainstorming, Document Analysis, Interviews, Lessons Learned, Process Modelling, Survey/Questionnaire, Workshops — "B-D-I-L-P-S-W"
  • Task 5 unique techniques: Metrics and KPIs, Observation, Process Analysis, Root Cause Analysis — all about measuring and diagnosing (fits the "improvement" purpose)
  • Task 1 unique techniques: Business Cases, Estimation, Financial Analysis — all about justifying the approach with numbers

6. PREDICTIVE vs. ADAPTIVE — Comparison Table

AspectPredictive (Plan-Driven)Adaptive (Change-Driven)
RequirementsDefined upfront, baselinedEvolve iteratively
DocumentationFormal, comprehensiveLightweight, just enough
Change controlFormal change requestsBacklog reprioritization
Stakeholder engagementScheduled formal reviewsContinuous collaboration
Sign-offMilestone-based approvalsAcceptance per iteration
TraceabilityDetailed matrixOften implicit in backlog
BA deliverablesBRD, SRS, use case docsUser stories, acceptance criteria
Risk approachUpfront risk analysisRisk addressed per iteration
When to useRegulatory, safety-critical, fixed scopeUncertain requirements, innovation

Exam tip: Questions often present a scenario and ask which approach is appropriate. Look for keywords:

  • "Regulatory compliance," "safety-critical," "fixed requirements" → Predictive
  • "Uncertain scope," "evolving needs," "frequent feedback" → Adaptive
  • "Parts of the system are well-understood, others are not" → Hybrid

7. STAKEHOLDER ROLES (Standard BABOK v3 List)

RoleDescriptionExam Notes
Business AnalystPlans and executes BA workCan be a person or team
CustomerUses or purchases the solutionNot always the end user
Domain SMEExpert in the business areaPrimary source for business requirements
End UserDirectly interacts with the solutionPrimary source for user requirements
Implementation SMEExpert in technology/buildHelps assess feasibility
Operational SupportMaintains the solution post-deliveryOften forgotten stakeholder
Project ManagerManages the projectCollaborates with BA on planning
RegulatorDefines compliance requirementsRequirements are non-negotiable
SponsorFunds and champions the initiativeHas final authority on scope/budget
SupplierProvides products/servicesExternal stakeholders
TesterValidates the solutionConsumes requirements for test cases

8. COMMON EXAM QUESTION PATTERNS FOR KA1

Pattern 1: "What should the BA do FIRST?"

Setup: New project/initiative starting. The BA needs to begin work.

Correct answer: Plan Business Analysis Approach

Why: It's the first task in KA1 and produces the approach that all other planning tasks depend on.

Common distractor: "Meet with stakeholders" — this feels right but stakeholder engagement is Task 2, which depends on the approach from Task 1.

Pattern 2: "Who should approve this requirement?"

Setup: A requirement needs approval, or there's a dispute about who has authority.

Correct answer: Refer to the Governance Approach

Why: Governance defines decision-making authority and approval processes.

Common distractor: "The sponsor" — while often true, the exam answer is about the process (governance), not the specific person.

Pattern 3: "The BA discovers requirements keep changing"

Setup: Frequent changes, scope creep, or unstable requirements.

Correct answer depends on nuance:

  • If asking about the process for handling changes → Governance Approach (change control)
  • If asking about tracking impact of changes → Information Management Approach (traceability)
  • If asking about whether the BA should change their methodology → Plan BA Approach (reassess predictive vs. adaptive)

Pattern 4: "How does the BA track relationships between requirements?"

Setup: Need to understand impact of changing one requirement on others.

Correct answer: Traceability (part of Information Management Approach)

Common distractor: "Requirements Life Cycle Management" — while RLCM uses traceability, the decision about how to do traceability is made in KA1, Task 4.

Pattern 5: "The BA's elicitation sessions are not producing useful results"

Setup: Quality problems in BA deliverables or processes.

Correct answer: Identify Business Analysis Performance Improvements (Task 5)

Common distractor: "Plan Stakeholder Engagement" (maybe the wrong people are in the room) — but the question is about assessing and improving BA performance, which is explicitly Task 5.

Pattern 6: "A new stakeholder is identified mid-project"

Setup: Someone who should have been involved wasn't included initially.

Correct answer: Update the Stakeholder Engagement Approach

Key insight: KA1 tasks are ITERATIVE. Plans are living documents that get updated throughout the initiative.

Pattern 7: "Predictive or Adaptive?"

Setup: Scenario describes a project context and asks what approach to use.

How to answer:

  • Count the signals: regulatory? fixed scope? safety? → Predictive
  • Uncertain? evolving? innovation? rapid feedback? → Adaptive
  • Mix of both? → Hybrid approach

9. KEY DEFINITIONS TO MEMORIZE

TermDefinitionDon't Confuse With
Business Analysis ApproachThe set of processes, templates, and activities for performing BA in a given contextProject management methodology
StakeholderAny individual or group with a relationship to the change, need, or solutionTeam member (stakeholders are broader)
GovernanceHow decisions about requirements are made, including approval and change controlInformation management
TraceabilityThe ability to track relationships between requirements and other elementsVersion control (that's configuration mgmt)
Requirements AttributeMetadata about a requirement (status, priority, source, owner, complexity)The requirement itself
Performance AssessmentEvaluation of BA process effectivenessSolution evaluation (that's KA6)

10. CROSS-KA CONNECTIONS (Exam Favorite)

KA1 outputs feed ALL other KAs:

KA1 OutputUsed InHow
BA ApproachAll KAsGuides how BA activities are performed
Stakeholder Engagement ApproachKA2 (Elicitation)Determines who to elicit from and how
Governance ApproachKA3 (RLCM)Controls requirement changes and approvals
Info Management ApproachKA3, KA4, KA5Defines how requirements are stored, traced, reused
BA Performance AssessmentKA1 (self)Feeds back into improving planning

Exam implication: If a question asks "What does the BA need BEFORE starting elicitation?" → The answer is likely one of the KA1 outputs (especially the BA Approach or Stakeholder Engagement Approach).

11. MNEMONICS AND MEMORY AIDS

5 Tasks in Order: "A-S-G-I-P" (Approach, Stakeholders, Governance, Information, Performance)

  • Think: "A Smart Governor Improves Performance"

5 Outputs: Remember each task produces an "approach" except Task 5:

  • Business Analysis Approach
  • Stakeholder Engagement Approach
  • Governance Approach
  • Information Management Approach
  • Business Analysis Performance Assessment ← the odd one out

Universal Techniques Mnemonic: "B-D-I-L-P-S-W"

  • Brainstorming, Document Analysis, Interviews, Lessons Learned, Process Modelling, Survey/Questionnaire, Workshops
  • Think: "Big Dogs In Lovely Parks Smell Wonderful"

BACCM Concepts: "C-N-S-S-V-C" = Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context

  • Think: "Can New Solutions Satisfy Various Concerns?"

12. RAPID-FIRE SELF-TEST (20 Questions)

1. What is the FIRST task in KA1?

Plan Business Analysis Approach

2. What is the only external input to KA1?

Needs

3. Which task defines how requirement changes are controlled?

Plan Business Analysis Governance

4. Which task addresses traceability?

Plan Business Analysis Information Management

5. Name the task that is self-referencing (its output feeds back as its own input).

Identify Business Analysis Performance Improvements

6. Stakeholder engagement is a TASK. Stakeholder analysis is a ___?

Technique

7. A BA is on a Scrum project. Should they use a predictive BA approach?

No — they should align with the adaptive methodology (but may use formal documentation for regulatory items)

8. Who defines the prioritization approach for requirements?

The Governance Approach (Task 3)

9. What are the 5 stakeholder analysis dimensions?

Authority, Influence, Attitude, Interest, Complexity of needs

10. Where are requirements attributes (status, priority, source) defined?

Information Management Approach (Task 4)

11. Name 3 techniques unique to Task 5.

Metrics and KPIs, Observation, Process Analysis, Root Cause Analysis (any 3)

12. A requirement changes and the BA needs to know what else is affected. What concept applies?

Traceability

13. Two VPs disagree on a requirement priority. Which task's output resolves this?

Governance Approach (conflict resolution is part of governance)

14. The BA is producing deliverables that stakeholders find too detailed. Which task should the BA revisit?

Plan Business Analysis Approach (level of formality and deliverables)

15. Name the 6 BACCM core concepts.

Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context

16. Is KA1 performed once at the start of a project?

No — all tasks are iterative and can be revisited throughout the initiative

17. What is the difference between BA Approach and BA Plan?

Approach = methodology/strategy; Plan = the collection of all planning outputs

18. A new regulation requires the BA to track all requirements to their source. Which task is most relevant?

Plan BA Information Management (traceability approach)

19. Name 3 universal techniques used across all 5 KA1 tasks.

Brainstorming, Document Analysis, Interviews, Lessons Learned, Process Modelling, Surveys, Workshops (any 3)

20. The BA's project retrospective reveals that requirements defects doubled compared to the last project. Which task addresses this?

Identify BA Performance Improvements

13. EXAM DAY QUICK REFERENCE

When you see these keywords in a question, think this task:

Keywords→ Task
methodology, approach, predictive, adaptive, formalityPlan BA Approach
stakeholder, engagement, collaboration, communication, RACIPlan Stakeholder Engagement
approval, authority, decision, change control, conflict, prioritizationPlan BA Governance
traceability, repository, storage, attributes, reuse, abstractionPlan BA Info Management
performance, improvement, effectiveness, measures, root causeIdentify BA Performance Improvements

The "FIRST" Rule:

If the question asks what the BA should do first when starting a new initiative:

  • Plan BA Approach (always first in KA1)
  • Then Stakeholder Engagement
  • Then Governance
  • Then Information Management
  • Performance Improvement is ongoing

The "Continuous" Rule:

All KA1 tasks can be revisited. If a question says "mid-project" and something changed:

→ The BA should UPDATE the relevant approach, not create a new one.

The "Which KA?" Decision Tree:

  • Planning HOW to do BA work → KA1
  • Drawing out information from stakeholders → KA2
  • Managing requirements lifecycle → KA3
  • Analyzing strategy and defining change → KA4
  • Analyzing and defining requirements and designs → KA5
  • Evaluating solution performance → KA6

Generated for CBAP exam preparation. Cross-reference with BABOK v3 Chapter 3 for page-level detail.

CBAP Cheat Sheet — KA2: Elicitation and Collaboration

Exam Weight: ~20% of exam questions. This is the second-highest weighted KA (after KA5: RADD at ~30%). Expect roughly 24 scenario-based questions directly testing KA2.

1. PURPOSE OF THIS KA

This KA defines how the BA draws out information from stakeholders and maintains ongoing collaboration throughout the initiative. It is NOT a one-time phase — elicitation happens continuously.

Critical exam distinction:

  • Elicitation = Drawing out, exploring, and identifying information relevant to the change
  • Collaboration = Working with stakeholders to ensure ongoing alignment
  • Elicitation ≠ Requirements gathering (BABOK avoids the word "gathering" — it implies information is sitting there waiting; elicitation means you actively draw it out)

2. THE 5 TASKS — Quick Reference

#TaskPrimary OutputCore Question
1Prepare for ElicitationElicitation Activity PlanWhat do we need before we start?
2Conduct ElicitationElicitation Results (Unconfirmed)How do we draw out information?
3Confirm Elicitation ResultsElicitation Results (Confirmed)Did we capture it correctly?
4Communicate Business Analysis InformationBusiness Analysis Information (Communicated)How do we share what we learned?
5Manage Stakeholder CollaborationStakeholder EngagementHow do we keep everyone working together?

3. TASK-BY-TASK DEEP DIVE

TASK 1: Prepare for Elicitation

Purpose: Ensure all needed resources are organized and scheduled for elicitation activities.

Inputs:

  • Needs (external)
  • Stakeholder Engagement Approach (from KA1, Task 2)
  • Business Analysis Approach (from KA1, Task 1)

Output:

  • Elicitation Activity Plan

Key Elements:

  • Understand the scope of the elicitation activity — what information do you need?
  • Select techniques based on:
  • Type of information needed
  • Stakeholder availability and preferences
  • Time and cost constraints
  • Organizational culture
  • Source of the business analysis information
  • Logistics: Schedule resources, location, tools, materials
  • Prepare stakeholders: Brief them on purpose, expectations, and any pre-work
  • Supporting materials: Gather existing documentation, templates, models

Techniques Used:

  • Brainstorming
  • Collaborative Games
  • Data Mining
  • Data Modelling
  • Document Analysis
  • Estimation
  • Interviews
  • Mind Mapping
  • Observation
  • Process Modelling
  • Reviews
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Survey or Questionnaire

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Preparation is a SEPARATE task — the BA must plan BEFORE conducting elicitation. If a question asks "What should the BA do BEFORE meeting stakeholders?" → Prepare for Elicitation.
  • The Elicitation Activity Plan is the OUTPUT, not the BA Approach. The BA Approach (from KA1) is an INPUT to this task.
  • "The BA is unsure which stakeholders to invite" → This means the Stakeholder Engagement Approach (from KA1) needs to be consulted or updated FIRST.
  • Supporting materials include existing documentation — don't skip Document Analysis during preparation.

TASK 2: Conduct Elicitation

Purpose: Draw out, explore, and identify information relevant to the change.

Inputs:

  • Elicitation Activity Plan (from Task 1)
  • Existing Business Analysis Information (from any KA)

Output:

  • Elicitation Results (Unconfirmed)

Key Elements — The 3 Types of Elicitation (MEMORIZE):

TypeDescriptionTechniquesKey Insight
CollaborativeDirect interaction with stakeholdersInterviews, Workshops, Focus Groups, Brainstorming, Collaborative GamesMost common; requires stakeholder availability
ResearchStudying existing information sourcesDocument Analysis, Interface Analysis, Data MiningNo direct stakeholder interaction needed
ExperimentsCreating new information through trialsPrototyping, Observation (of process), Proof of ConceptDiscovers things not knowable through asking or reading

Critical Elements:

  • Guide the elicitation — keep it on track, manage time, address tangents
  • Capture results — notes, recordings, whiteboards, models
  • Sponsor support — sponsor can help engage reluctant stakeholders
  • Manage unexpected outcomes — new stakeholders discovered, scope revealed to be larger than expected

Techniques Used:

  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Brainstorming
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Collaborative Games
  • Concept Modelling
  • Data Mining
  • Data Modelling
  • Document Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interface Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Mind Mapping
  • Observation
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Prototyping
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • The output is Elicitation Results (UNCONFIRMED) — NOT confirmed. Confirmation happens in Task 3. This is a heavily tested distinction.
  • "The BA observes the end users performing their daily tasks" → This is Conduct Elicitation using the Observation technique, classified as an EXPERIMENT type.
  • "The BA reads existing system documentation" → This is Conduct Elicitation using Document Analysis, classified as RESEARCH type.
  • "A stakeholder mentions a new requirement during an interview" → The BA captures it as elicitation results and follows up — they do NOT immediately add it to the requirements. It must go through confirmation first.
  • Prototyping is used DURING Conduct Elicitation, not during Confirm Elicitation Results.

TASK 3: Confirm Elicitation Results

Purpose: Check the information gathered during elicitation for accuracy and consistency with other information.

Inputs:

  • Elicitation Results (Unconfirmed) — from Task 2
  • Existing Business Analysis Information

Output:

  • Elicitation Results (Confirmed)

Key Elements:

  • Compare information — cross-reference with what was already known, check against multiple sources
  • Identify errors and omissions — find gaps, conflicts, ambiguities early
  • Gain shared understanding — ensure stakeholders and the BA agree on what was captured
  • Correct early — fixing misunderstandings during confirmation is much cheaper than later

What Confirmation is NOT:

  • NOT formal approval/sign-off (that's Governance in KA1/KA3)
  • NOT validation of requirements against business needs (that's KA5)
  • NOT verification of requirements quality (that's also KA5)
  • It IS simply: "Did we capture what you said correctly?"

Techniques Used:

  • Document Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Reviews
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Confirm ≠ Approve. Confirmation checks ACCURACY of captured information. Approval authorizes requirements for use. If a question mentions "sign-off" or "authorization" → that's governance/approval, not confirmation.
  • Confirm ≠ Validate. Validation checks if requirements deliver VALUE. Confirmation checks if you HEARD correctly.
  • The output state changes from "Unconfirmed" to "Confirmed" — exam questions love testing this state transition.
  • "After the workshop, the BA sends meeting notes to attendees for review" → This is Confirm Elicitation Results (checking accuracy).
  • "Two stakeholders gave conflicting information" → Discovered during confirmation (comparing sources). BA needs to resolve this, potentially through additional elicitation.

TASK 4: Communicate Business Analysis Information

Purpose: Ensure stakeholders have a shared understanding of business analysis information.

Inputs:

  • Business Analysis Information (from any KA — not just elicitation results)
  • Stakeholder Engagement Approach (from KA1, Task 2)

Output:

  • Business Analysis Information (Communicated)

Key Elements:

  • Determine audience — who needs what information?
  • Tailor the message — format, level of detail, and presentation style based on stakeholder needs
  • Executives → high-level summaries, dashboards, business cases
  • Developers → detailed specs, models, technical requirements
  • End users → process flows, wireframes, plain language
  • Select communication method:
  • Formal: presentations, written documents, sign-off packages
  • Informal: emails, conversations, chat messages
  • Group: workshops, presentations, demos
  • Individual: one-on-one meetings, emails
  • Packaging: Organize information into logical, consumable packages

Techniques Used:

  • Interviews
  • Reviews
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • This task communicates ALL business analysis information, not just elicitation results. Models, requirements, analysis results — anything the BA produces.
  • "The BA presents a prototype to the steering committee" → Communicate BA Information (sharing analyzed/packaged info with specific audience).
  • Don't confuse this with Confirm Elicitation Results — communication is about SHARING info broadly; confirmation is about CHECKING accuracy with the source.
  • "The BA tailors documentation for different audiences" → Communicate BA Information.
  • The Requirements Traceability Matrix can be communicated as part of this task — but it's CREATED in KA1 Task 4 / KA3.
  • A common distractor is "Manage Stakeholder Collaboration." Communication is one-way sharing; collaboration is two-way working together.

TASK 5: Manage Stakeholder Collaboration

Purpose: Encourage stakeholders to work together toward a common goal and manage their engagement.

Inputs:

  • Stakeholder Engagement Approach (from KA1, Task 2)
  • Business Analysis Information (Communicated) — from Task 4

Output:

  • Stakeholder Engagement

Key Elements:

  • Gain agreement on commitments — stakeholders agree to dedicate time and effort
  • Monitor engagement — track whether stakeholders are fulfilling their roles
  • Manage conflicts — address disagreements between stakeholders
  • Risk assessment — identify engagement risks (key stakeholder leaving, resistance increasing)
  • Improve collaboration — find ways to work more effectively together

Techniques Used:

  • Collaborative Games
  • Lessons Learned
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Collaboration ≠ Communication. Communication = sharing information. Collaboration = working TOGETHER (two-way).
  • "A key stakeholder is not attending scheduled workshops" → Manage Stakeholder Collaboration (monitoring and addressing engagement).
  • "Two department heads disagree about a process" → Manage Stakeholder Collaboration (conflict management). But if they disagree about requirement PRIORITY → that's Governance (KA1 Task 3).
  • "The BA needs the sponsor to encourage stakeholder participation" → Manage Stakeholder Collaboration (sponsor helps with engagement).
  • This is an ONGOING task, not a one-time event. It runs continuously alongside all BA activities.

4. INPUTS AND OUTPUTS — MASTER MAP


From KA1:
  Business Analysis Approach ──┐
  Stakeholder Engagement Approach ──┤
                                    │
Needs (external) ──────────────────┤
                                    ↓
                        ┌── Prepare for Elicitation ──→ Elicitation Activity Plan
                        │                                       │
                        │                                       ↓
                        │         Conduct Elicitation ──→ Elicitation Results (UNCONFIRMED)
                        │                                       │
                        │                                       ↓
                        │     Confirm Elicitation Results ──→ Elicitation Results (CONFIRMED)
                        │                                       │
                        │                                       ↓
    BA Information ←────┤  Communicate BA Information ──→ BA Information (Communicated)
    (from any KA)       │                                       │
                        │                                       ↓
                        └── Manage Stakeholder Collaboration ──→ Stakeholder Engagement

Key insight: Elicitation Results go through TWO states:

  • Unconfirmed — raw output from Conduct Elicitation
  • Confirmed — validated for accuracy through Confirm Elicitation Results

The confirmed results then feed into KA3 (RLCM), KA4 (Strategy Analysis), and KA5 (RADD).

5. THE 3 TYPES OF ELICITATION — Deep Dive

This classification is an exam favorite. Know which techniques fall under each type.

Collaborative Elicitation

Definition: Involves direct interaction between the BA and stakeholders.

When to use: When you need to understand stakeholder needs, concerns, perspectives.

TechniqueBest ForKey Consideration
InterviewsDeep exploration with 1-2 peopleCan be structured, semi-structured, or unstructured
WorkshopsGroup elicitation, consensus buildingRequires a facilitator (may or may not be the BA)
Focus GroupsGetting reactions from a representative groupGroup dynamics can influence responses
BrainstormingGenerating many ideas quicklyDefer judgment; quantity over quality initially
Collaborative GamesCreative exploration, breaking down barriersEngages reluctant stakeholders; uncovers hidden assumptions

Research Elicitation

Definition: Studying existing materials and systems without direct stakeholder interaction.

When to use: When stakeholders are unavailable, when documenting current state, when analyzing existing systems.

TechniqueBest ForKey Consideration
Document AnalysisUnderstanding existing processes, policies, regulationsDocuments may be outdated or incomplete
Interface AnalysisUnderstanding system interactionsUseful for integration requirements
Data MiningDiscovering patterns in existing dataRequires access to data and analytical tools

Experiments

Definition: Creating new information that cannot be discovered through asking or reading.

When to use: When requirements are uncertain, when stakeholders can't articulate needs, when testing feasibility.

TechniqueBest ForKey Consideration
PrototypingValidating UI/UX, discovering hidden requirementsCan be throwaway or evolutionary
ObservationUnderstanding real workflows (not documented ones)People may behave differently when observed (Hawthorne effect)
Proof of ConceptTesting technical feasibilityNot the same as a prototype

6. ELICITATION TECHNIQUES — Comparison Matrix

TechniqueTypeStakeholder InteractionBest forLimitations
InterviewsCollaborativeHigh (1-2 people)Detailed exploration, sensitive topicsTime-consuming, one perspective at a time
WorkshopsCollaborativeHigh (group)Consensus, multiple perspectives at onceRequires skilled facilitation, scheduling challenge
Focus GroupsCollaborativeMedium (selected group)Reactions, attitudes, preferencesGroupthink risk, dominant personalities
BrainstormingCollaborativeHigh (group)Idea generationNeeds facilitation to avoid evaluation too early

Survey/QuestionnaireCollaborativeLow (asynchronous)Large populations, quantitative dataLow response rates, can't probe deeply

Memory tricks:

  • Task 3 (Confirm) has the FEWEST techniques (4): Document Analysis, Interviews, Reviews, Workshops — "D-I-R-W" — because confirmation is focused: you're checking, not exploring.
  • Task 4 (Communicate) also has few techniques (3): Interviews, Reviews, Workshops — same as T3 minus Document Analysis.
  • Task 2 (Conduct) has the MOST techniques (18) — because elicitation is where you use the widest variety of methods.
  • Prototyping is ONLY in Task 2 (Conduct) — not in Confirm or Communicate.

8. ELICITATION RESULTS — STATE MANAGEMENT

This is one of the most tested concepts in KA2. Understand the state transitions:


Conduct Elicitation
        │
        ↓
Elicitation Results (UNCONFIRMED)
        │
        │ ← Confirm Elicitation Results
        ↓
Elicitation Results (CONFIRMED)
        │
        ├──→ KA3: Requirements Life Cycle Management
        ├──→ KA4: Strategy Analysis
        ├──→ KA5: Requirements Analysis and Design Definition
        └──→ KA6: Solution Evaluation

Exam question patterns:

  • "What state are the results in immediately after a workshop?" → Unconfirmed
  • "Before the BA can start analyzing requirements, what state must elicitation results be in?" → Confirmed (confirmed results are inputs to other KAs)
  • "The BA discovered an inconsistency between interview notes and workshop output" → This happens during Confirm Elicitation Results (comparing sources)

9. STAKEHOLDER ROLES IN KA2

StakeholderRole in Elicitation
Business AnalystPlans, facilitates, and conducts elicitation; confirms and communicates results
Domain SMEPrimary source of business knowledge — key elicitation target
End UserProvides information about daily operations and needs
CustomerProvides perspective on external expectations
SponsorAuthorizes access to stakeholders; helps engage reluctant participants
Project ManagerCoordinates scheduling and resource availability
Implementation SMEProvides technical feasibility input
RegulatorProvides compliance requirements (often through documents, not interviews)
TesterMay participate to understand requirements early

Exam tip: The Sponsor's role in elicitation is specifically about AUTHORIZING and HELPING ENGAGE — they typically don't provide requirements themselves.

10. COMMON EXAM QUESTION PATTERNS FOR KA2

Pattern 1: "What should the BA do BEFORE the elicitation session?"

Setup: The BA has a workshop/interview/observation planned.

Correct answer: Prepare for Elicitation (Task 1)

Key activities: Define scope, select technique, schedule resources, prepare materials, brief stakeholders.

Common distractor: "Conduct Elicitation" — wrong; preparation must come first.

Pattern 2: "The BA just completed a series of interviews. What should they do NEXT?"

Setup: Elicitation is done, results are captured.

Correct answer: Confirm Elicitation Results (Task 3)

Why: Results are unconfirmed until verified for accuracy and consistency.

Common distractor: "Analyze requirements" — wrong; results must be confirmed before analysis (which is KA5).

Pattern 3: "Which type of elicitation is being used?"

Setup: Scenario describes a specific activity.

How to answer:

  • Talking to people (interviews, workshops, games) → Collaborative
  • Reading documents, analyzing data, studying interfaces → Research
  • Building prototypes, observing users, running proof of concept → Experiments

Pattern 4: "Confirm vs. Validate vs. Verify vs. Approve"

Setup: Scenario asks what the BA should do with requirements/information.

Critical distinctions:

TermKAWhat it ChecksQuestion it Answers
ConfirmKA2 (Task 3)Accuracy of captured information"Did I hear you correctly?"
VerifyKA5 (RADD)Quality and correctness of requirements"Is this requirement well-written and complete?"
ValidateKA5 (RADD)Alignment with business needs and value"Will this requirement deliver the expected value?"
ApproveKA3 (RLCM) / KA1 GovernanceAuthorization to proceed"Are we authorized to move forward with this?"

This 4-way distinction is one of the most common CBAP exam traps.

Pattern 5: "The BA needs to communicate requirements to different audiences"

Setup: Different stakeholders need different formats/levels of detail.

Correct answer: Communicate Business Analysis Information (Task 4)

Key: Tailor the message — executives get summaries, developers get specs, users get process flows.

Common distractor: "Manage Stakeholder Collaboration" — wrong; communication is about sharing, collaboration is about working together.

Pattern 6: "A stakeholder is disengaged/resistant/absent"

Setup: Collaboration problem.

Correct answer: Manage Stakeholder Collaboration (Task 5)

Potential actions: Involve the sponsor, reassess engagement approach, address root cause of resistance.

Common distractor: "Plan Stakeholder Engagement" (KA1 Task 2) — this is about PLANNING engagement; managing collaboration is about EXECUTING and MONITORING it.

Pattern 7: "Which elicitation technique should the BA use?"

Setup: Scenario with constraints (time, geography, number of stakeholders, type of information needed).

Decision guide:

ConstraintBest Technique
Need deep detail from one personInterview
Need consensus from groupWorkshop
Stakeholders geographically dispersedSurvey/Questionnaire
Need to understand real (not documented) processObservation
Requirements are vague/unclearPrototyping
Existing systems must be understoodDocument Analysis, Interface Analysis
Large amount of historical dataData Mining
Need creative ideasBrainstorming, Collaborative Games
Need reactions from representative groupFocus Group

Pattern 8: "New information surfaces during elicitation"

Setup: Unexpected finding — new stakeholder, new requirement, scope change.

Correct answer depends on context:

  • New stakeholder found → Update Stakeholder Engagement Approach (KA1)
  • New requirement area discovered → May need additional elicitation (back to Task 1: Prepare)
  • Conflict between sources → Resolve during Confirm Elicitation Results (Task 3)

Key principle: Elicitation is ITERATIVE. Go back to earlier tasks as needed.

11. KEY DEFINITIONS TO MEMORIZE

TermDefinitionDon't Confuse With
ElicitationDrawing out, exploring, and identifying information relevant to the changeRequirements gathering (implies passive collection)
Elicitation Results (Unconfirmed)Raw output from an elicitation activity, not yet verifiedConfirmed results (verified for accuracy)
Elicitation Results (Confirmed)Results verified for accuracy and consistencyApproved requirements (authorized by governance)
Collaborative ElicitationDirect interaction with stakeholdersResearch (no direct interaction)
Research ElicitationStudying existing materials and systemsCollaborative (requires direct interaction)
ExperimentsCreating new information through trialsPrototyping specifically (experiments is the category)
ObservationWatching stakeholders perform tasks to understand real workflowsInterview (observation is watching, not asking)
FacilitationGuiding a group activity to achieve a productive outcomeLeading (facilitators guide, not direct)

12. CROSS-KA CONNECTIONS (Exam Favorites)

KA2 ElementConnects ToHow
Elicitation Activity PlanKA1 outputs are inputs to Task 1BA Approach and Stakeholder Engagement Approach guide preparation
Elicitation Results (Confirmed)KA3, KA4, KA5, KA6Confirmed results feed into all downstream analysis
Stakeholder EngagementKA1 Task 2, Task 5Planned in KA1, managed in KA2
CommunicationAll KAsCommunication happens throughout all BA work
Techniques (e.g., Interviews)KA1, KA3, KA5Same techniques used across multiple KAs for different purposes

Exam implication: "What input does the BA need before starting elicitation?" → Stakeholder Engagement Approach and BA Approach (both from KA1).

13. PREDICTIVE vs. ADAPTIVE — Impact on KA2

AspectPredictiveAdaptive
Elicitation timingUpfront, scheduled phasesContinuous, per iteration/sprint
Documentation levelDetailed meeting notes, formal reportsLightweight: user stories, acceptance criteria
ConfirmationFormal review cyclesOngoing during iteration
CommunicationFormal packages, review meetingsDaily standups, demos, backlog grooming
Stakeholder collaborationScheduled touchpointsContinuous (product owner embedded in team)
Technique preferenceInterviews, Document Analysis, WorkshopsBrainstorming, Collaborative Games, Prototyping

14. MNEMONICS AND MEMORY AIDS

5 Tasks in Order: "P-C-C-C-M" (Prepare, Conduct, Confirm, Communicate, Manage)

  • Think: "Please Can Cats Catch Mice?"

3 Elicitation Types: "C-R-E" (Collaborative, Research, Experiments)

  • Think: "CREate knowledge" through collaboration, research, and experiments

Confirm vs. Validate vs. Verify: "C = Captured, Ve = Value, Vi = Valid quality"

  • Confirm: "Did I capture what you said?"
  • Validate: "Does this deliver value?"
  • Verify: "Is this of good quality?"

State Transitions: "Unconfirmed → Confirmed → Analyzed → Approved"

  • Think of it like a manufacturing quality pipeline — raw material → inspected → processed → shipped

15. RAPID-FIRE SELF-TEST (25 Questions)

1. What is the FIRST task in KA2?

Prepare for Elicitation

2. Name the 3 types of elicitation.

Collaborative, Research, Experiments

3. What is the output state of Conduct Elicitation?

Elicitation Results (Unconfirmed)

4. What is the difference between Confirm and Validate?

Confirm = checking accuracy of captured info; Validate = checking alignment with business value

5. Which task produces Elicitation Results (Confirmed)?

Confirm Elicitation Results (Task 3)

6. A BA sends workshop notes to attendees for review. Which task is this?

Confirm Elicitation Results

7. A BA presents a requirements package to the steering committee. Which task?

Communicate Business Analysis Information

8. Which elicitation type does Observation fall under?

Experiments

9. Which elicitation type does Document Analysis fall under?

Research

10. Which elicitation type does an Interview fall under?

Collaborative

11. A key stakeholder refuses to participate. Which task addresses this?

Manage Stakeholder Collaboration

12. How many techniques does Task 3 (Confirm) use?

4: Document Analysis, Interviews, Reviews, Workshops

13. Which task has the MOST techniques?

Task 2: Conduct Elicitation (18 techniques)

14. Name 2 inputs to Prepare for Elicitation from KA1.

Business Analysis Approach, Stakeholder Engagement Approach

15. The BA discovers that existing process documentation is outdated. What type of elicitation was being used?

Research (Document Analysis)

16. "Sign-off on requirements" belongs to which task/KA?

Approve Requirements in KA3 (RLCM), not KA2

17. Can elicitation happen during Solution Evaluation (KA6)?

Yes — elicitation is not a phase; it occurs continuously across all KAs as needed

18. What role does the Sponsor play in Conduct Elicitation?

Authorizes access to stakeholders and helps engage reluctant participants

19. A BA tailors a presentation for executives differently than for developers. Which task?

Communicate Business Analysis Information

20. Two stakeholders gave conflicting descriptions of the same process. Which task discovers this?

Confirm Elicitation Results (comparing information from multiple sources)

21. Prototyping is a technique for which task(s) in KA2?

Conduct Elicitation only (Task 2)

22. What is the Hawthorne effect and which technique is it relevant to?

People change behavior when they know they're being observed — relevant to Observation technique

23. The BA needs information from 500 end users spread across 10 countries. Best technique?

Survey/Questionnaire (scalable, asynchronous, geographic reach)

24. The BA wants to understand how the current system integrates with external systems. Best technique?

Interface Analysis (Research type)

25. Is KA2 performed only at the beginning of a project?

No — elicitation and collaboration are continuous and iterative throughout the initiative

16. EXAM DAY QUICK REFERENCE

When you see these keywords in a question, think this task:

Keywords→ Task
prepare, plan activity, schedule, logistics, supporting materialsPrepare for Elicitation
interview, observe, workshop, elicit, draw out, discoverConduct Elicitation
verify accuracy, check consistency, review notes, compare sourcesConfirm Elicitation Results
present, share, package, tailor message, audience, formatCommunicate BA Information
engage, participate, commitment, conflict, collaborate, monitor engagementManage Stakeholder Collaboration

The State Transition Rule:

  • After conducting → results are UNCONFIRMED
  • After confirming → results are CONFIRMED
  • Only CONFIRMED results should feed into analysis tasks in other KAs

The "What NEXT?" Rule:

If the question describes an elicitation activity that was JUST completed:

  • ✓ Captured information → Next: Confirm Elicitation Results
  • ✓ Confirmed information → Next: Communicate or feed into analysis (KA5)
  • ✗ Found gaps/conflicts → Next: Go back and conduct MORE elicitation

The 4-Way Distinction (highest exam ROI concept):

  • Confirm = captured correctly (KA2)
  • Verify = meets quality standards (KA5)
  • Validate = delivers value (KA5)
  • Approve = authorized to proceed (KA3/governance)

content:
CBAP Cheat Sheet — KA3: Requirements Life Cycle Management (RLCM)

Exam Weight: ~16% of exam questions. Expect roughly 19 scenario-based questions. RLCM is the "backbone" KA — it determines how requirements are maintained, controlled, and governed from inception to retirement.

1. PURPOSE OF THIS KA

This KA defines how the BA manages requirements and designs throughout their entire lifecycle. It covers tracing, maintaining, prioritizing, assessing changes, and approving requirements.

Critical exam distinction:

  • KA1 (Planning) = PLANNING how to manage requirements (defining the approach)
  • KA3 (RLCM) = EXECUTING requirement management (actually doing it)
  • KA5 (RADD) = ANALYZING and DEFINING requirements (creating/refining the content)
  • KA3 does NOT create requirements — it manages their lifecycle once they exist

Key principle: RLCM tasks are NOT sequential phases. They happen continuously throughout the initiative.

2. THE 5 TASKS — Quick Reference

#TaskPrimary OutputCore Question
1Trace RequirementsRequirements (Traced)How do requirements relate to each other?
2Maintain RequirementsRequirements (Maintained)Are requirements still accurate and current?
3Prioritize RequirementsRequirements (Prioritized)Which requirements matter most?
4Assess Requirements ChangesRequirements Change AssessmentWhat is the impact of this change?
5Approve RequirementsRequirements (Approved)Are we authorized to move forward?

3. TASK-BY-TASK DEEP DIVE

TASK 1: Trace Requirements

Purpose: Ensure requirements and designs at different levels are aligned and manage the effects of change across levels.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)

Output:

  • Requirements (Traced)

Key Elements:

  • Traceability relationships — linking requirements to other requirements, designs, solution components, and test cases
  • Levels of traceability:
  • Business Requirements ↔ Stakeholder Requirements ↔ Solution Requirements ↔ Transition Requirements
  • Traceability enables:
  • Impact analysis (what else changes when this requirement changes?)
  • Coverage analysis (are all business needs addressed by solution requirements?)
  • Allocation (which solution component implements which requirement?)
  • Gap detection (are there requirements without a parent or orphaned items?)

The 4 Traceability Relationships (MEMORIZE):

RelationshipDirectionMeaningExample
DeriveParent → ChildRequirement B is derived from Requirement ABusiness Req → Stakeholder Req
DependPeer → PeerRequirement B depends on Requirement ALogin required before placing an order
SatisfyComponent → RequirementSolution component satisfies a requirementDatabase module satisfies data storage req
CoverTest → RequirementTest case covers a requirementTest case TC-042 covers REQ-015

Techniques Used:

  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Data Flow Diagrams
  • Data Modelling
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interaction Modelling
  • Item Tracking
  • Process Modelling
  • Scope Modelling

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Traceability is about RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN requirements, not about the requirements themselves.
  • "A new regulation affects multiple system requirements" → Use traceability to perform IMPACT ANALYSIS (trace backward from regulation to find all affected requirements).
  • The DECISION about how to do traceability is made in KA1 Task 4 (Information Management). The EXECUTION of traceability is KA3 Task 1.
  • Forward tracing (need → requirement → design → implementation) and backward tracing (implementation → design → requirement → need) are both needed.
  • Orphaned requirements (no parent) and gold-plating (solution features with no traced requirement) are detected through traceability analysis.

TASK 2: Maintain Requirements

Purpose: Keep requirements accurate and consistent throughout their lifecycle, and support reuse.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)

Output:

  • Requirements (Maintained)

Key Elements:

  • Accuracy: Ensure requirements reflect current understanding (correct errors, update outdated info)
  • Consistency: Remove conflicts between requirements
  • Reuse: Identify requirements that can be reused across initiatives
  • Long-lived requirements (regulations, business rules, data standards) are prime reuse candidates
  • Reusable requirements should be stored in a requirements repository
  • Requirements attributes maintenance: Keep metadata (status, priority, source, owner) up to date
  • Representation and abstraction: Ensure requirements are at the right level of detail for their audience

Requirement States (know these):


Stated → Confirmed → Drafted → Approved → Traced → Validated → Prioritized → Implemented → Verified
                                                                                              ↓
                                                                                           Retired

Note: BABOK v3 does NOT prescribe a single fixed set of states — it depends on the organization. Common states include:

  • Active — currently valid and in use
  • Deferred — postponed to a future release
  • Cancelled — no longer relevant
  • Implemented — built into the solution
  • Verified — tested and confirmed working

Techniques Used:

  • Data Modelling
  • Document Analysis
  • Interface Analysis
  • Item Tracking
  • Process Modelling
  • Use Cases and Scenarios
  • User Stories

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Maintaining requirements is ONGOING, not a one-time task. Requirements evolve.
  • "A requirement was approved 3 months ago but the business process has since changed" → The requirement needs to be MAINTAINED (updated for accuracy).
  • Reuse ≠ Copy-paste. Reusable requirements must be general enough to apply across contexts and must be stored in a managed repository.
  • Requirements attributes (status, priority, source) are DEFINED in KA1 Task 4 but MAINTAINED here in KA3 Task 2.
  • Don't confuse Maintain with Assess Changes — Maintain is about keeping requirements accurate; Assess Changes is about evaluating the impact of a PROPOSED change.

TASK 3: Prioritize Requirements

Purpose: Rank requirements based on their relative importance to determine implementation order and resource allocation.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)

Output:

  • Requirements (Prioritized)

Key Elements:

  • Basis for prioritization (know all of these):
FactorDescriptionExample Question
BenefitValue delivered to stakeholders"How much revenue does this generate?"
PenaltyConsequence of NOT implementing"What happens if we skip this?"
CostEffort/resources to implement"How expensive is this to build?"
RiskUncertainty or potential for failure"How technically risky is this?"
DependenciesRelationships requiring specific order"Does anything else need this first?"
Time sensitivityUrgency or regulatory deadlines"Is there a legal deadline?"
StabilityHow likely the requirement is to change"Will this requirement keep changing?"
Stakeholder agreementLevel of consensus"Do all parties agree on this?"
  • Who prioritizes: Stakeholders prioritize (not the BA alone). The BA FACILITATES prioritization.
  • Conflict resolution: When stakeholders disagree on priority, refer to the Governance Approach (KA1 Task 3).

Prioritization Techniques (exam favorites):

TechniqueHow It WorksBest For
MoSCoWMust Have / Should Have / Could Have / Won't Have (this time)Timeboxed projects, Agile
Timeboxing/BudgetingAllocate requirements to fixed time/budget slotsIterative/release planning
VotingStakeholders vote on prioritiesQuick consensus with many stakeholders
RankingOrder requirements from most to least importantSmall requirement sets
Weighted CriteriaScore requirements against multiple factorsComplex multi-factor decisions
Decision AnalysisFormal evaluation against defined criteriaHigh-stakes decisions

Techniques Used (BABOK list):

  • Backlog Management
  • Business Cases
  • Decision Analysis
  • Estimation
  • Financial Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • MoSCoW Analysis
  • Multivoting
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Timeboxing
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • The BA facilitates prioritization, NOT decides it. Stakeholders own the priority decisions. The BA presents information and manages the process.
  • Prioritization is CONTINUOUS. Priorities change as the project evolves — especially in Adaptive approaches where backlog reprioritization happens every iteration.
  • "Two VPs disagree on which requirement is more important" → Refer to the Governance Approach for conflict resolution, NOT reprioritize yourself.
  • Don't confuse Prioritize (KA3) with the Prioritization Approach in KA1 — KA1 PLANS the prioritization approach; KA3 EXECUTES it.
  • MoSCoW: "Won't Have" means "Won't Have THIS TIME" — not "never." It's explicitly deferred, not cancelled.

TASK 4: Assess Requirements Changes

Purpose: Evaluate the impact of proposed changes to requirements and designs.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)
  • Proposed Change (external — from any stakeholder)

Output:

  • Requirements Change Assessment

Key Elements:

  • Impact analysis: What else is affected by this change?
  • Use traceability to find all related requirements, designs, and solution components
  • Assess impact on scope, schedule, budget, quality, and risk
  • Evaluate against business objectives: Does the change still align with the original need?
  • Cost-benefit analysis: Is the change worth the effort?
  • Formality depends on approach:
  • Predictive: Formal change request process, documented impact analysis, change control board
  • Adaptive: Backlog reprioritization, assessed in sprint planning, lighter-weight process
  • Recommend action: Accept, reject, defer, or request more information

Techniques Used:

  • Business Cases
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Estimation
  • Financial Analysis
  • Interface Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Scope Modelling
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Assess Changes ≠ Approve Changes. Assessment is ANALYSIS of impact; Approval is the DECISION to proceed. They are separate tasks.
  • "A stakeholder submits a change request" → The BA first ASSESSES the impact (Task 4), THEN the change goes for APPROVAL (Task 5).
  • The BA does NOT approve or reject changes alone. The BA assesses and recommends; stakeholders (per governance) approve.
  • Traceability (Task 1) is essential for impact analysis — you can't assess a change properly if you can't trace what it affects.
  • In Adaptive, this may be as simple as evaluating a new user story against the product backlog. In Predictive, it's a formal change control process.

TASK 5: Approve Requirements

Purpose: Obtain agreement and approval from stakeholders to proceed with requirements and designs.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)
  • Requirements Change Assessment (from Task 4, if applicable)

Output:

  • Requirements (Approved)

Key Elements:

  • Who approves: Defined in the Governance Approach (KA1 Task 3) — typically sponsors, business owners, or designated approvers
  • What approval means:
  • Agreement that requirements are complete enough to proceed
  • Authorization to use approved requirements for downstream work (design, build, test)
  • NOT a guarantee that requirements won't change later
  • Conflict resolution: When stakeholders can't agree, escalate per governance process
  • Tracking decisions: Record approvals, including who approved, when, and any conditions
  • Types of approval:
  • Consensus — all parties agree
  • Majority vote — most parties agree
  • Deferral to authority — designated approver decides
  • Unanimous — all must agree (rare, used for critical/regulatory requirements)

Techniques Used:

  • Decision Analysis
  • Item Tracking
  • Reviews
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Approve ≠ Confirm ≠ Validate ≠ Verify. This 4-way distinction (also covered in KA2) is heavily tested:
TermKAWhat it ChecksQuestion it Answers
ConfirmKA2Accuracy of captured information"Did I hear correctly?"
VerifyKA5Quality and correctness of requirements"Is this well-written?"
ValidateKA5Alignment with business value/needs"Will this deliver value?"
ApproveKA3Authorization to proceed"Are we allowed to move forward?"
  • Approval can be CONDITIONAL (e.g., "approved pending resolution of item X").
  • Approval can be REVOKED if circumstances change — requirements can be "un-approved" and sent back for reassessment.
  • In Adaptive: approval often happens informally (product owner accepts a user story); in Predictive: formal sign-off meetings.
  • "The BA finalized requirements and needs authorization to start design" → Approve Requirements (Task 5).

4. INPUTS AND OUTPUTS — MASTER MAP


Requirements & Designs (from KA2 confirmed results, KA5 analysis)
    │
    ├──→ Trace Requirements ──→ Requirements (Traced)
    │                               │
    ├──→ Maintain Requirements ──→ Requirements (Maintained)
    │                               │
    ├──→ Prioritize Requirements ──→ Requirements (Prioritized)
    │                               │
    │    Proposed Change ──→ Assess Requirements Changes ──→ Requirements Change Assessment
    │                                                           │
    └──→ Approve Requirements ←─────────────────────────────────┘
              │
              ↓
         Requirements (Approved) ──→ KA5 (RADD) / Implementation / Testing

Key insight: These 5 tasks are NOT linear. They operate in parallel and iteratively:

  • You trace WHILE you maintain
  • You prioritize THROUGHOUT the project
  • Changes can occur at ANY time
  • Approval may happen incrementally (per iteration) or at milestones

5. REQUIREMENTS HIERARCHY — The 4 Levels

This hierarchy is tested extensively across KA3 and other KAs. Know it cold.

LevelWhat It CapturesCreated ByExample
Business RequirementsStrategic goals, objectives, outcomesSponsor, executives"Reduce customer churn by 20%"
Stakeholder RequirementsNeeds of specific stakeholder groupsDomain SMEs, users, customers"Customer service reps need to see full order history"
Solution RequirementsWhat the solution must doBA, implementation SMESplit into: Functional + Non-functional
Transition RequirementsTemporary needs for migrationBA, operational support"Historical data must be migrated before go-live"

Solution Requirements break down into:

  • Functional: What the system DOES (features, functions, behaviors)
  • Non-functional (Quality of Service): How the system PERFORMS (speed, security, availability, usability)

Traceability between levels:


Business Requirements
        ↓ (derive)
Stakeholder Requirements
        ↓ (derive)
Solution Requirements (Functional + Non-functional)
        ↓ (derive)
Transition Requirements

⚠️ EXAM TRAP: Transition Requirements are TEMPORARY — they exist only to support the transition from current to future state and can be retired after go-live.

6. TECHNIQUES MAPPED TO TASKS

TechniqueT1 TraceT2 MaintainT3 PrioritizeT4 Assess ChangesT5 Approve
Backlog Management✓
Business Cases✓✓
Business Rules Analysis✓✓
Data Flow Diagrams✓
Data Modelling✓✓
Decision Analysis✓✓✓
Document Analysis✓✓
Estimation✓✓
Financial Analysis✓✓
Functional Decomposition✓
Interaction Modelling✓
Interface Analysis✓✓
Interviews✓✓
Item Tracking✓✓✓✓✓
MoSCoW Analysis✓
Multivoting✓
Process Modelling✓✓
Reviews✓
Risk Analysis and Management✓✓
Scope Modelling✓✓
Timeboxing✓
Use Cases and Scenarios✓
