Workshops✓✓✓

Memory tricks:

  • Item Tracking appears in ALL 5 tasks — because you're always tracking requirements throughout the lifecycle.
  • Task 3 (Prioritize) has the MOST techniques (12) — because prioritization involves the broadest analysis.
  • Task 5 (Approve) has the FEWEST techniques (4): Decision Analysis, Item Tracking, Reviews, Workshops — "D-I-R-W" — because approval is focused on decision-making.
  • Task 1 (Trace) is heavy on modelling techniques (Data Modelling, Process Modelling, Scope Modelling, Functional Decomposition) — because tracing requires understanding structure.

7. PREDICTIVE vs. ADAPTIVE — Impact on KA3

AspectPredictiveAdaptive
TraceabilityFormal traceability matrix, detailed coverage analysisOften implicit in backlog structure; lighter-weight
MaintenanceControlled document updates with version controlContinuous backlog grooming/refinement
PrioritizationUpfront prioritization, formal change to re-prioritizeContinuous backlog reprioritization per iteration
Change assessmentFormal change request, change control board reviewNew story assessed against backlog in sprint planning
ApprovalFormal sign-off at milestones (requirements baseline)Product owner accepts stories per iteration
Change controlHeavy: formal process, impact analysis, CCB approvalLight: backlog reordering, sprint negotiation
BaselineRequirements baselined, changes tracked from baselineNo formal baseline; backlog is living document

Exam keywords:

  • "Change control board," "requirements baseline," "formal sign-off" → Predictive
  • "Product backlog," "sprint planning," "continuous reprioritization" → Adaptive

8. REQUIREMENTS STATES AND LIFECYCLE FLOW

Requirements don't just exist — they move through states. While BABOK v3 doesn't mandate specific state names, the concept of state transitions is heavily tested.

Common State Flow:


Elicited (raw, unconfirmed)
    ↓
Confirmed (accuracy checked — KA2)
    ↓
Analyzed/Modeled (specified — KA5)
    ↓
Traced (relationships mapped — KA3 T1)
    ↓
Prioritized (ranked — KA3 T3)
    ↓
Approved (authorized — KA3 T5)
    ↓
Implemented (built — external)
    ↓
Verified (tested — external)
    ↓
[Active | Deferred | Cancelled | Retired]

State-Change Triggers:

  • New information discovered → Re-elicit, re-confirm
  • Business change → Assess change impact, may need re-approval
  • Priority shift → Re-prioritize
  • Error found → Maintain (correct and update)
  • Solution retired → Requirements retired

9. TRACEABILITY MATRIX — Quick Reference

The traceability matrix is the primary tool for Task 1. Know its structure:

Req IDRequirementSourceBusiness ReqStakeholder ReqSolution ReqTest CaseStatusPriority
BR-001Reduce churn 20%CEO—SR-001, SR-002——ApprovedMust
SR-001See full order historyCSR teamBR-001—SOL-001TC-042ApprovedMust
SOL-001Order history APIArchitectBR-001SR-001—TC-042, TC-043PrioritizedMust

What the matrix enables:

  • Impact analysis: Change BR-001 → trace forward to find all affected SR and SOL requirements
  • Coverage analysis: Are all BR requirements covered by at least one SR and SOL?
  • Gap detection: Any SOL requirement with no parent SR? That's gold-plating.
  • Orphan detection: Any SR with no parent BR? That's an orphan — investigate.

10. COMMON EXAM QUESTION PATTERNS FOR KA3

Pattern 1: "A stakeholder requests a change to an approved requirement"

Setup: Change proposed after approval.

Correct answer sequence:

  • Assess Requirements Changes (Task 4) — analyze impact
  • Present assessment to decision-makers
  • Approve Requirements (Task 5) — decision to accept/reject
  • If accepted: Maintain (Task 2) and re-Trace (Task 1)

Common distractor: "Immediately update the requirement" — wrong; assess impact first.

Pattern 2: "The BA needs to determine which requirements to include in the next release"

Setup: Limited resources, need to choose.

Correct answer: Prioritize Requirements (Task 3)

Techniques: MoSCoW, Timeboxing, Decision Analysis

Common distractor: "Approve Requirements" — approval is about authorization, not selection for a release.

Pattern 3: "A change in one requirement affects several others"

Setup: Ripple effect of a change.

Correct answer: Use traceability (Task 1) to perform impact analysis

Why: Traceability maps the relationships, so you can identify all affected requirements.

Common distractor: "Maintain Requirements" — maintenance updates the content; traceability identifies WHAT to update.

Pattern 4: "Who decides the priority of requirements?"

Setup: Conflict or ambiguity about who makes priority decisions.

Correct answer: Stakeholders (as defined in the Governance Approach from KA1 Task 3)

Key: The BA FACILITATES prioritization. The BA does NOT prioritize alone.

Common distractor: "The business analyst" or "the project manager."

Pattern 5: "Requirements need to be signed off before development begins"

Setup: Formal approval required.

Correct answer: Approve Requirements (Task 5)

Context: This is typical in Predictive approaches. In Adaptive, approval may be product owner accepting stories.

Common distractor: "Validate Requirements" (KA5) — validation checks alignment with value, NOT authorization.

Pattern 6: "An old requirement is no longer relevant"

Setup: Requirement should be retired or cancelled.

Correct answer: Maintain Requirements (Task 2) — update the status to retired/cancelled

Why: Maintaining includes keeping requirement states current.

Common distractor: "Delete the requirement" — requirements should NOT be deleted; their status should be changed to maintain audit trail.

Pattern 7: "The BA needs to ensure all business needs are addressed by solution requirements"

Setup: Gap analysis / coverage analysis.

Correct answer: Trace Requirements (Task 1) — check for complete coverage

Why: Tracing reveals whether every business requirement has derived solution requirements.

Common distractor: "Validate Requirements" (KA5) — validation checks value alignment, not structural coverage.

Pattern 8: "Requirements were approved but keep changing"

Setup: Unstable requirements, scope creep.

Correct answer depends on nuance:

  • If asking about the process → Governance Approach (change control from KA1)
  • If asking about the specific change → Assess Requirements Changes (Task 4)
  • If asking about whether the BA approach is right → Revisit Plan BA Approach (KA1 Task 1)

11. KEY DEFINITIONS TO MEMORIZE

TermDefinitionDon't Confuse With
TraceabilityAbility to track relationships between requirements and other elements at different levelsVersion control (tracking changes over time)
Requirements BaselineApproved set of requirements at a point in time, used as reference for change controlCurrent requirements (may differ from baseline after changes)
Impact AnalysisAssessment of the effect a change to one requirement has on othersRisk analysis (broader; impact analysis is specific to a change)
Requirements ReuseApplying existing requirements to new initiativesCopy-paste (reuse requires managed, generalized requirements)
Gold PlatingAdding solution features not traced to any requirementScope creep (uncontrolled growth); gold plating is unnecessary extras
Orphan RequirementA requirement with no parent/sourceDerived requirement (which HAS a parent)
Change ControlProcess for managing changes to approved requirementsVersion control (technical; change control is governance)
MoSCoWMust Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have (this time)Simple ranking (MoSCoW categorizes, not ranks)

12. CROSS-KA CONNECTIONS (Exam Favorites)

KA3 ElementConnects ToHow
Trace RequirementsKA1 Task 4 (Info Management)Traceability approach is PLANNED in KA1, EXECUTED in KA3
Prioritize RequirementsKA1 Task 3 (Governance)Prioritization approach defined in governance; executed here
Approve RequirementsKA1 Task 3 (Governance)Approval authority and process defined in governance
Assess ChangesKA1 Task 3 (Governance)Change control process defined in governance
Requirements (Approved)KA5 (RADD)Approved requirements feed into analysis and design work
Requirements (Approved)KA6 (Solution Eval)Approved requirements are the benchmark for evaluating the solution
Requirements (Traced)KA2 (Elicitation)Confirmed elicitation results become inputs to traceability

Exam implication: KA3 is the BRIDGE between KA1 (planning) and KA5/KA6 (analysis/evaluation). Without RLCM, planning has no execution and analysis has no controlled inputs.

13. MNEMONICS AND MEMORY AIDS

5 Tasks in Order: "T-M-P-A-A" (Trace, Maintain, Prioritize, Assess, Approve)

  • Think: "Tracing Makes Prioritization And Approval" possible

4 Traceability Relationships: "D-D-S-C" (Derive, Depend, Satisfy, Cover)

  • Think: "Derived Dependencies Satisfy Coverage"

8 Prioritization Factors: "B-P-C-R-D-T-S-S" (Benefit, Penalty, Cost, Risk, Dependencies, Time sensitivity, Stability, Stakeholder agreement)

  • Think: "Big Projects Cost Resources, Demanding Time, Skill, Support"

MoSCoW: Must / Should / Could / Won't (this time)

  • Remember: the "o"s are lowercase and just spacers. "W" = Won't have THIS TIME (not "never")

4 Requirement Levels: "B-S-S-T" (Business, Stakeholder, Solution, Transition)

  • Think: "Business Stakeholders Seek Transitions"

14. RAPID-FIRE SELF-TEST (25 Questions)

1. What are the 5 tasks in KA3?

Trace, Maintain, Prioritize, Assess Changes, Approve

2. Name the 4 traceability relationships.

Derive, Depend, Satisfy, Cover

3. What is the difference between Approve and Validate?

Approve = authorization to proceed (KA3); Validate = checking value alignment (KA5)

4. Who is responsible for prioritizing requirements?

Stakeholders prioritize; the BA facilitates the process

5. A requirement has no parent business requirement. What is this called?

Orphan requirement

6. A solution feature exists with no traced requirement. What is this called?

Gold plating

7. Name the 4 levels of requirements.

Business, Stakeholder, Solution (Functional + Non-functional), Transition

8. Which KA PLANS the traceability approach?

KA1 Task 4 (Plan BA Information Management)

9. Which KA EXECUTES traceability?

KA3 Task 1 (Trace Requirements)

10. A stakeholder submits a change request. What does the BA do FIRST?

Assess Requirements Changes (Task 4) — analyze the impact before seeking approval

11. What does MoSCoW stand for?

Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have (this time)

12. What is a requirements baseline?

An approved set of requirements at a point in time, used as a reference for change control

13. Which technique is present in ALL 5 KA3 tasks?

Item Tracking

14. In an Agile project, how is prioritization typically handled?

Continuous backlog reprioritization by the product owner

15. A change to a business requirement needs to be analyzed. Which task comes first: Trace or Assess?

Trace (you need traceability to identify what's affected BEFORE you can assess impact)

16. Are KA3 tasks performed sequentially?

No — they are performed continuously and iteratively throughout the initiative

17. An old requirement is no longer relevant. Should the BA delete it?

No — change its status to retired/cancelled to maintain the audit trail (Maintain Requirements)

18. What is the primary tool for performing impact analysis?

Traceability matrix

19. Which task has the fewest techniques?

Approve Requirements (4 techniques: Decision Analysis, Item Tracking, Reviews, Workshops)

20. Transition Requirements are different from other requirements because they are ___.

Temporary — they exist only to support the transition from current to future state

21. Name 3 factors used to prioritize requirements.

Benefit, Penalty, Cost, Risk, Dependencies, Time sensitivity, Stability, Stakeholder agreement (any 3)

22. The BA discovers two requirements that conflict with each other. Which task applies?

Maintain Requirements (resolve conflicts to keep requirements consistent)

23. A requirement was approved. Can it be un-approved?

Yes — approval can be revoked if circumstances change; the requirement goes back for reassessment

24. What is the difference between forward and backward traceability?

Forward: Need → Requirement → Design → Implementation; Backward: Implementation → Design → Requirement → Need

25. Which KA3 task uses MoSCoW Analysis?

Prioritize Requirements (Task 3)

15. EXAM DAY QUICK REFERENCE

When you see these keywords in a question, think this task:

Keywords→ Task
relationships, alignment, impact analysis, coverage, derive, depend, satisfy, cover, matrixTrace Requirements
accuracy, consistency, reuse, repository, attributes, status update, retire, currentMaintain Requirements
rank, order, MoSCoW, benefit, cost, risk, release planning, backlog, must/should/couldPrioritize Requirements
change request, impact, cost-benefit, proposed change, what-if, ripple effectAssess Requirements Changes
sign-off, authorization, consensus, approval, proceed, baseline, accept/rejectApprove Requirements

The Change Request Sequence:

When a change is proposed:

  • Trace — identify what's affected using traceability
  • Assess — analyze the impact (cost, benefit, risk, scope)
  • Present — communicate assessment to decision-makers
  • Approve/Reject — governance decides
  • Maintain — if approved, update the requirement and its attributes
  • Re-Trace — update traceability relationships

The "Who Decides?" Rule:

  • BA facilitates — presents information, runs the process
  • Stakeholders decide — per the Governance Approach from KA1
  • Never: "The BA decides the priority/approval alone"

KA3 vs. Other KAs Decision Guide:

  • "How should we manage requirements?" → KA1 (Planning)
  • "Let's gather requirements from stakeholders" → KA2 (Elicitation)
  • "Let's trace/maintain/prioritize/change-control/approve requirements" → KA3 (RLCM)
  • "Let's analyze the business strategy and define the future state" → KA4 (Strategy)
  • "Let's model and specify the requirements in detail" → KA5 (RADD)
  • "Let's evaluate if the solution delivers value" → KA6 (Solution Eval)

Generated for CBAP exam preparation. Cross-reference with BABOK v3 Chapter 5 for page-level detail.

Sources: IIBA BABOK Guide v3 task cards, AdaptiveUS exam guidance, Watermark Learning, ModernRequirements, TrustedInstitute, ExamZify (content rephrased for compliance with licensing restrictions).
title: KA3 — Requirements Life Cycle Management

content:
CBAP Cheat Sheet — KA4: Strategy Analysis

Exam Weight: ~15% of exam questions. Expect roughly 18 scenario-based questions. Strategy Analysis is the "WHY" KA — it answers why the change is needed, what the future should look like, and how to get there.

1. PURPOSE OF THIS KA

This KA defines how the BA identifies the business need, analyzes the current and future states, assesses risks, and defines a change strategy. It operates at the STRATEGIC level — above individual requirements.

Critical exam distinction:

  • KA4 (Strategy Analysis) = WHY change is needed and WHAT the future looks like (strategic direction)
  • KA5 (RADD) = WHAT specifically must be built (detailed requirements and design)
  • KA6 (Solution Evaluation) = DID the solution deliver value (post-implementation assessment)
  • KA4 happens BEFORE or AT THE BEGINNING of the project lifecycle, though it can be revisited

Key principle: Strategy Analysis produces the BUSINESS REQUIREMENTS and CHANGE STRATEGY that drive all downstream BA work.

2. THE 4 TASKS — Quick Reference

#TaskPrimary OutputCore Question
1Analyze Current StateCurrent State DescriptionWhere are we now and why do we need to change?
2Define Future StateFuture State DescriptionWhere do we want to be?
3Assess RisksRisk Analysis ResultsWhat could go wrong?
4Define Change StrategyChange StrategyHow do we get from here to there?

Note: KA4 has only 4 tasks (all other KAs have 5). This is worth remembering for the exam.

3. TASK-BY-TASK DEEP DIVE

TASK 1: Analyze Current State

Purpose: Understand the business need and how it relates to the way the enterprise currently functions. Sets a baseline and context for change.

Inputs:

  • Elicitation Results (Confirmed) — from KA2
  • Needs (external — from sponsor, market, or regulatory driver)

Output:

  • Current State Description

Key Elements:

  • Business Need: Why does the organization need to change?
  • Problem to solve ("customer complaints are rising 30% quarterly")
  • Opportunity to capture ("new market segment worth €50M")
  • Compliance mandate ("new regulation effective in 12 months")
  • Organizational assessment:
  • Structure and culture
  • Capabilities and processes
  • Technology and infrastructure
  • Policies and business rules
  • External influences (market, competitors, regulations)
  • Internal assets: People, systems, data, intellectual property
  • Stakeholder concerns: Different groups may view the current state differently

Elements of Current State Description:

ElementWhat It IncludesExample
Business NeedThe driver for change"Customer retention dropped 15%"
Organizational StructureHow the org is arrangedDepartments, reporting lines, geographic distribution
CapabilitiesWhat the org can doSkills, systems, processes currently in place
TechnologyCurrent systems and toolsLegacy CRM, manual spreadsheet processes
Policies/RulesCurrent constraints"All orders over €10,000 require VP approval"
External InfluencesOutside factorsCompetitor launched new product; new EU regulation
Internal AssetsResources availableStaff expertise, existing data, infrastructure

Techniques Used:

  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Capability Analysis
  • Business Model Canvas
  • Business Cases
  • Concept Modelling
  • Data Mining
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Scope Modelling
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • SWOT Analysis
  • Vendor Assessment
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Analyzing the current state is NOT just documenting "as-is" processes. It includes understanding WHY change is needed (the business need).
  • "The BA is tasked with understanding why the organization needs a new system" → Analyze Current State (Task 1).
  • Root Cause Analysis is used HERE (to understand the underlying problem), NOT in KA5 or KA6.
  • SWOT Analysis is a technique for this task — used to assess the current state's Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats.
  • Don't confuse current state analysis with solution evaluation (KA6). Current state = before the change. Solution evaluation = after the change.
  • "Multiple departments describe the same process differently" → This is discovered during current state analysis. The BA must reconcile differing views.

TASK 2: Define Future State

Purpose: Define the set of conditions required to meet the business need and define the success of the initiative.

Inputs:

  • Current State Description (from Task 1)
  • Elicitation Results (Confirmed) — from KA2

Output:

  • Future State Description

Key Elements:

  • Business Goals and Objectives:
  • Goals = broad, qualitative ("improve customer satisfaction")
  • Objectives = specific, measurable ("achieve 90% customer satisfaction score by Q4")
  • SMART objectives: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
  • Solution Scope: What is IN scope and what is OUT of scope for the solution
  • Includes organizational structures, skills, technology, processes, infrastructure, policies
  • Constraints: Limitations on the solution space
  • Budget, timeline, technology, regulatory, organizational
  • Success Metrics: How will we measure whether the future state is achieved?
  • Dependencies: What else must be in place for the future state to work?
  • Potential Value: Expected benefits (quantified where possible)

Techniques Used:

  • Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria
  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Capability Analysis
  • Business Cases
  • Business Model Canvas
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Metrics and KPIs
  • Mind Mapping
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Scope Modelling
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • SWOT Analysis
  • Vendor Assessment
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • The future state is NOT the solution. It's the DESIRED CONDITION. The solution is how you achieve the future state.
  • "The BA defines business goals and measurable objectives" → Define Future State (Task 2).
  • Goals vs. Objectives is a critical distinction:
  • Goal: "Improve efficiency" (qualitative, broad)
  • Objective: "Reduce processing time by 40% within 6 months" (SMART)
  • "What is the solution scope?" → Defined here in Task 2, NOT in KA5.
  • The future state includes NON-TECHNICAL elements: organizational structure changes, new skills needed, policy updates, process redesigns.
  • Don't assume future state = new system. It could be a process change, organizational restructuring, or policy update with no technology involved.

TASK 3: Assess Risks

Purpose: Understand the potential negative consequences of the change during transition to, or in, the future state, and recommend a response.

Inputs:

  • Current State Description (from Task 1)
  • Future State Description (from Task 2)
  • Elicitation Results (any state) — from KA2

Output:

  • Risk Analysis Results

Key Elements:

  • Risk identification: What events could occur that would negatively affect the change?
  • Risks to the TRANSITION (getting from current to future state)
  • Risks IN the future state (ongoing risks after implementation)
  • Risk analysis dimensions:
DimensionDescriptionExample
LikelihoodProbability the risk will occur"High — vendor has missed deadlines before"
ImpactSeverity if the risk occurs"Critical — would delay go-live by 3 months"
TimeframeWhen the risk might occur"During data migration phase"
  • Risk tolerance: Organization's willingness to accept risk (risk-averse vs. risk-tolerant)
  • Risk response strategies (MEMORIZE):
StrategyActionWhen to Use
AvoidEliminate the risk entirely by changing the approachWhen the risk is too severe and can be prevented
TransferShift the risk to a third party (insurance, outsourcing)When someone else can manage it better
MitigateReduce the likelihood or impactWhen the risk can't be avoided but can be controlled
AcceptAcknowledge the risk and take no proactive actionWhen the cost of response exceeds the potential impact
  • Risk categorization: Technical, organizational, business, external
  • Stakeholder risk tolerance: Different stakeholders may have different risk appetites

Techniques Used:

  • Business Cases
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Risk Analysis and Management ← primary technique
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Risk assessment happens BEFORE defining the change strategy. You must understand the risks to make informed strategic decisions.
  • "The BA identifies that the proposed approach has a high risk of failure" → Assess Risks (Task 3), then factor into Change Strategy (Task 4).
  • Risk is about NEGATIVE consequences. Opportunities (positive outcomes) are addressed in Current/Future State analysis.
  • Don't confuse with Risk Analysis and Management (a technique) vs. Assess Risks (a task). The technique is USED WITHIN the task.
  • Risk tolerance varies by stakeholder. The sponsor might accept high risk for high reward; the regulator might accept zero risk.
  • "The organization is considering two approaches with different risk profiles" → Assess Risks for both, then compare in Define Change Strategy.

TASK 4: Define Change Strategy

Purpose: Perform gap analysis between current and future states, evaluate options, and recommend the approach to achieve the future state.

Inputs:

  • Current State Description (from Task 1)
  • Future State Description (from Task 2)
  • Risk Analysis Results (from Task 3)
  • Elicitation Results (Confirmed) — from KA2

Output:

  • Change Strategy

Key Elements:

  • Gap Analysis (core activity):
  • Compare current state to future state
  • Identify what needs to change (capabilities, processes, technology, people, policies)
  • Assess the magnitude of the gaps
  • Solution Approach:
  • Define the breadth and depth of the solution
  • Consider alternatives (build vs. buy vs. configure; full replacement vs. incremental improvement)
  • Evaluate each option against criteria (cost, benefit, risk, feasibility, time)
  • Transition States:
  • If the change is too large for a single step, define intermediate states
  • Each transition state delivers partial value while moving toward the future state
  • Think of these as "phases" or "releases"
  • Solution Scope refinement: Narrow down what the solution will and won't address
  • Organizational readiness: Is the organization ready for this change?
  • Training needs
  • Cultural change
  • Stakeholder buy-in
  • Resource availability
  • Financial analysis: Cost-benefit, ROI, NPV, payback period

Elements of the Change Strategy:

ElementDescription
Gap AnalysisWhat must change between current and future state
Solution ApproachHow the change will be implemented (build, buy, etc.)
Transition StatesIntermediate steps between current and future state
Release PlanningHow the solution will be delivered in phases
Organizational ReadinessAssessment of the org's ability to absorb the change
DependenciesWhat else must happen for the strategy to succeed
Cost-BenefitFinancial justification for the recommended approach

Techniques Used:

  • Balanced Scorecard
  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Capability Analysis
  • Business Cases
  • Business Model Canvas
  • Decision Analysis
  • Estimation
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Scope Modelling
  • SWOT Analysis
  • Vendor Assessment
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Gap analysis is the HEART of Define Change Strategy. Current state vs. future state = gaps = what needs to change.
  • "The BA compares the current capabilities with what's needed" → Gap Analysis within Define Change Strategy (Task 4).
  • Transition states are KEY for large changes. The exam loves scenarios where the change is too big for one step.
  • "The organization wants to replace their legacy system but can't do it all at once" → Define transition states (phased rollout).
  • Build vs. Buy is a decision made HERE, not in KA5. KA5 defines detailed options AFTER the strategic approach is set.
  • Organizational readiness assessment happens HERE — the BA evaluates whether the org can handle the proposed change.
  • Don't confuse Change Strategy with Change Control (KA3). Strategy = the plan for the change. Control = managing changes to requirements.
  • "The BA recommends implementing in three phases" → Define Change Strategy (transition states / release planning).

4. INPUTS AND OUTPUTS — MASTER MAP


Needs (external) ──┐
                    │
Elicitation Results ──┤
(Confirmed)           │
                      ↓
              Analyze Current State ──→ Current State Description
                      │                        │

                      │                        │

                        Detailed requirements    Solution performance
                        and design work          benchmarks

Key insight: KA4 is largely SEQUENTIAL (unlike other KAs). You generally:

  • Understand where you are (Current State)
  • Define where you want to be (Future State)
  • Understand what could go wrong (Risks)
  • Determine how to get there (Change Strategy)

However, you CAN iterate — discovering risks may cause you to revisit the future state definition.

5. THE GAP ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK

Gap analysis is the central analytical activity in KA4. Know this framework inside out.


CURRENT STATE                          FUTURE STATE
┌─────────────────┐                    ┌─────────────────┐
│ Capabilities    │ ←── GAP ──→       │ Required         │
│ Processes       │                    │ Capabilities     │
│ Technology      │                    │ New Processes    │
│ People/Skills   │                    │ New Technology   │
│ Policies        │                    │ New Skills       │
│ Culture         │                    │ New Policies     │
└─────────────────┘                    └─────────────────┘
         │                                      │
         └────────── GAPS IDENTIFIED ───────────┘
                          │
                          ↓
                  CHANGE STRATEGY
                  (How to close the gaps)
                          │
                    ┌─────┴──────┐
                    ↓            ↓
            Transition     Transition
            State 1        State 2 → Future State

Gap categories:

  • Capability gaps: What the org can't do but needs to
  • Process gaps: Current processes that don't support the future state
  • Technology gaps: Missing or inadequate systems
  • People/Skills gaps: Training, hiring, or reorganization needed
  • Policy gaps: Rules that must change
  • Cultural gaps: Mindset or behavioral changes required

6. CURRENT STATE vs. FUTURE STATE — Comparison Table

DimensionCurrent State AnalysisFuture State Definition
FocusWhere we are nowWhere we want to be
Business NeedIdentified and analyzedAddressed by the future state
GoalsN/A (current state IS the baseline)Defined and measurable (SMART)

ConstraintsExisting limitationsNew constraints identified
RisksExisting problems/vulnerabilitiesRisks of the change assessed separately (Task 3)
TechniquesSWOT, Root Cause Analysis, Process AnalysisBenchmarking, Business Model Canvas, Decision Analysis
OutputCurrent State DescriptionFuture State Description

7. RISK RESPONSE STRATEGIES — Deep Dive

StrategyDefinitionExampleWhen to Use
AvoidChange plans to eliminate the risk"Use proven technology instead of cutting-edge"High likelihood + High impact
TransferShift risk ownership to a third party"Outsource data migration to specialist vendor"When others can manage it better/cheaper
MitigateTake action to reduce likelihood or impact"Add extra testing phase; create rollback plan"Medium risks that can be controlled
AcceptAcknowledge the risk, no proactive action"Accept that some users may resist the change"Low impact risks; cost of response > impact
EscalateRaise to a higher authority for decision"Escalate regulatory risk to the steering committee"When the risk is beyond the BA's/team's authority

Exam tip: Questions often present a scenario and ask which risk strategy the BA should recommend. Match the response to the risk's likelihood, impact, and the organization's risk tolerance.

Memory tricks:

  • Universal techniques (all 4 tasks): Business Cases, Financial Analysis, Interviews, Item Tracking, Lessons Learned, Mind Mapping, Risk Analysis and Management, Workshops — "B-F-I-I-L-M-R-W"
  • Task 1 unique techniques: Concept Modelling, Data Mining — these are about understanding EXISTING reality
  • Task 2 unique techniques: Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria, Metrics and KPIs — these are about defining SUCCESS measures
  • Task 4 unique techniques: Balanced Scorecard, Estimation — these are about PLANNING the change
  • SWOT appears in Tasks 1, 2, and 4 but NOT in Task 3 (Assess Risks) — because SWOT is a strategic assessment tool, not purely a risk tool
  • Root Cause Analysis appears in Tasks 1 and 3 — understanding WHY problems exist (current state) and WHY risks exist

9. STRATEGY ANALYSIS CONCEPTS — Deep Dive

Business Need Categories

Problem/Pain PointSomething wrong that must be fixed"Order processing errors costing €2M/year"Internal quality issues
OpportunityPotential for improvement or growth"New market segment could generate €50M"Market changes
ComplianceRegulatory or legal mandate"GDPR requires data portability by deadline"External regulation

Business Case Components

Financial Analysis Techniques (know these for exam)

10. COMMON EXAM QUESTION PATTERNS FOR KA4

Pattern 1: "The organization has a problem. What should the BA do FIRST?"

Setup: New initiative, problem identified but not yet analyzed.

Correct answer: Analyze Current State (Task 1)

Why: You must understand the current situation before defining where to go.

Common distractor: "Define the solution" — wrong; strategy before solution.

Pattern 2: "The BA has documented the current state. What's next?"

Setup: Current state analysis complete.

Correct answer: Define Future State (Task 2)

Why: With the baseline established, define where you want to be.

Common distractor: "Start gathering requirements" (KA2/KA5) — wrong; you need the strategic direction first.

Pattern 3: "The BA is comparing the current and future states"

Setup: Both states defined, now looking at what needs to change.

Correct answer: Define Change Strategy (Task 4) — specifically the gap analysis element

Why: Gap analysis is the core of the change strategy, comparing current vs. future.

Common distractor: "Assess Risks" — while risks are assessed, gap analysis is part of defining the change strategy.

Pattern 4: "Which risk response should the BA recommend?"

Setup: Specific risk scenario with details about likelihood, impact, and organizational context.

How to answer:

  • Very high impact, can be prevented → Avoid
  • Better managed by someone else → Transfer
  • Can be reduced with action → Mitigate
  • Cost of response > potential impact → Accept
  • Beyond the team's authority → Escalate

Pattern 5: "Build vs. Buy?"

Setup: Organization needs a new capability and is evaluating options.

Correct answer: This decision is made during Define Change Strategy (Task 4)

Evaluation criteria: Cost, time-to-value, customization needs, vendor reliability, long-term maintenance, risk

Common distractor: "Define Solution Options" (KA5) — KA5 defines DETAILED options after the strategic direction is set. Build vs. Buy is a STRATEGIC decision.

Pattern 6: "The change is too large for a single implementation"

Setup: Complex change requiring phased delivery.

Correct answer: Define Transition States within Define Change Strategy (Task 4)

Key: Each transition state should deliver partial value while moving toward the future state.

Common distractor: "Prioritize Requirements" (KA3) — while prioritization helps, the STRATEGIC decision about phasing is made in KA4.

Pattern 7: "What is the difference between a Goal and an Objective?"

Setup: Definitional question, often embedded in a scenario.

Answer:

  • Goal: Qualitative, broad, directional ("improve customer experience")
  • Objective: Quantitative, SMART, measurable ("achieve NPS score of 75 by Q4 2027")

Common distractor: Using them interchangeably — they are DIFFERENT concepts.

Pattern 8: "The BA discovers the root cause of the business problem"

Setup: Problem analysis during current state assessment.

Correct answer: Analyze Current State (Task 1) — using Root Cause Analysis technique

Why: Understanding the root cause is part of understanding the current state.

Common distractor: "Assess Risks" — root cause analysis IS used in risk assessment too, but for understanding WHY a PROBLEM exists, it's Task 1.

11. KEY DEFINITIONS TO MEMORIZE

TermDefinitionDon't Confuse With
Business NeedA problem, opportunity, or constraint that drives the changeBusiness requirement (the formal statement of the need)
Current StateThe existing situation before the changeAs-is process (just one element of current state)
Future StateThe desired conditions after the changeSolution (how you get there); Future state is the destination
Gap AnalysisComparing current state to future state to identify what must changeVariance analysis (comparing actual to planned performance)
Change StrategyThe recommended approach to move from current to future stateChange control (managing changes to requirements — KA3)
Transition StateAn intermediate state between current and future stateRelease (a transition state may encompass multiple releases)
RiskAn uncertain event that could negatively affect the changeIssue (something that HAS happened; risk is something that MIGHT happen)
Solution ScopeThe boundary of what the solution will addressProject scope (broader; includes schedule, budget, resources)
SMART ObjectiveSpecific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-boundGoal (qualitative and broad)
Business CaseA document justifying the investment in the changeFeasibility study (narrower; assesses whether it CAN be done)

Future State DescriptionKA5 (RADD)Provides the strategic context for detailed requirements
Change StrategyKA5 (RADD)Drives solution option definition

Exam implication: KA4 is the BRIDGE between the business (why change) and the project (what to build). If a question asks about strategic decisions before requirements are defined → KA4.

13. PREDICTIVE vs. ADAPTIVE — Impact on KA4

AspectPredictiveAdaptive
Current state analysisThorough upfront; formal documentationMay be lighter; evolves with understanding
Future state definitionDetailed upfront; formal business caseHigh-level vision; refined per iteration
Risk assessmentFormal risk register; upfront analysisRisks assessed per iteration; lighter-weight

Gap analysisOne-time comprehensive analysisOngoing; gaps refined as solution emerges

14. MNEMONICS AND MEMORY AIDS

4 Tasks in Order: "C-F-R-C" (Current, Future, Risks, Change)

  • Think: "Current Facts Reveal Changes"

4 Risk Responses: "A-T-M-A" (Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept)

  • Think: "ATM Always" works — just like an ATM gives you options for how to handle your money

Gap Analysis = Current State – Future State = What Must Change

  • Think: The "gap" is what's MISSING between where you are and where you want to be

SMART Objectives: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound

  • Standard mnemonic — just know it cold

Business Need Triggers: "P-O-C-S" (Problem, Opportunity, Compliance, Strategic initiative)

  • Think: "POCS — What POKED the organization to change?"

Financial Techniques: "R-N-P-I-C" (ROI, NPV, Payback, IRR, Cost-Benefit)

  • Think: "Return Now Pays Investors Cash"

15. RAPID-FIRE SELF-TEST (25 Questions)

1. How many tasks does KA4 have?

4 (the only KA with 4 instead of 5)

2. What is the FIRST task in KA4?

Analyze Current State

3. What is a Business Need?

A problem, opportunity, or constraint that drives the change

4. Name the 4 risk response strategies.

Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept

5. What is a gap analysis?

Comparing current state to future state to identify what must change

6. What is the difference between a Goal and an Objective?

Goal = qualitative, broad; Objective = quantitative, SMART

7. Where does the Build vs. Buy decision happen?

Define Change Strategy (Task 4)

8. What is a transition state?

An intermediate state between current and future state that delivers partial value

9. Which technique is used to understand WHY a problem exists?

Root Cause Analysis (used in Task 1: Analyze Current State)

10. What does SWOT stand for?

Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats

11. Where is the solution scope defined?

Define Future State (Task 2)

12. The organization can't implement the full change at once. What should the BA define?

Transition states within the Change Strategy

13. What is the difference between Risk and Issue?

Risk = uncertain event that MIGHT happen; Issue = something that HAS happened

14. Name 3 components of a Business Case.

Needs assessment, desired outcomes, solution options, cost-benefit, risk assessment, recommendation (any 3)

15. Which task produces the Change Strategy?

Define Change Strategy (Task 4)

16. What technique identifies Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats?

SWOT Analysis

17. A new regulation requires the organization to change its process. What type of business need is this?

Compliance mandate

18. NPV stands for what?

Net Present Value

19. The BA discovers that the organization lacks the skills needed for the new system. What type of gap is this?

People/Skills gap (identified during gap analysis in Task 4)

20. Don't confuse Change Strategy (KA4) with what?

Change Control (KA3) — Strategy = plan for the change; Control = managing changes to requirements

21. What are the inputs to Assess Risks (Task 3)?

Current State Description, Future State Description, Elicitation Results

22. "The vendor might not deliver on time" — is this a risk or an issue?

Risk (it hasn't happened yet — it's uncertain)

23. Is KA4 performed only before the project starts?

No — it can be revisited throughout the initiative, though it typically happens early

24. What financial technique shows when cumulative benefits equal cumulative costs?

Payback Period

25. The BA recommends outsourcing a risky integration to a specialist firm. Which risk strategy is this?

Transfer

16. EXAM DAY QUICK REFERENCE

When you see these keywords in a question, think this task:

Keywords→ Task
business need, root cause, current situation, as-is, existing, capabilities, SWOTAnalyze Current State
goals, objectives, SMART, scope, constraints, vision, desired outcomes, futureDefine Future State
risk, likelihood, impact, tolerance, avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, negative eventAssess Risks
gap analysis, transition, phases, build/buy, approach, readiness, cost-benefit, releaseDefine Change Strategy

The Sequential Flow:

Unlike other KAs, KA4 generally flows in order:

  • Current State (where are we?) → 2. Future State (where do we want to be?) → 3. Risks (what could go wrong?) → 4. Change Strategy (how do we get there?)

The "Strategic vs. Tactical" Rule:

  • Strategic decisions (WHAT to change, WHY to change) → KA4
  • Tactical decisions (HOW to implement specific requirements) → KA5
  • Evaluation decisions (DID the solution work) → KA6

The 3-Way Distinction:

  • Current State = where you ARE
  • Future State = where you WANT to be
  • Change Strategy = HOW you GET there (including gap analysis and transition states)

title: KA4 — Strategy Analysis

content:
CBAP Cheat Sheet — KA5: Requirements Analysis and Design Definition (RADD)

Exam Weight: ~30% of exam questions — the HEAVIEST knowledge area. Expect roughly 36 scenario-based questions. This is where the exam hits hardest. Master this KA and you've covered nearly a third of the exam.

1. PURPOSE OF THIS KA

This KA defines how the BA structures, organizes, specifies, models, verifies, validates, and refines requirements and designs — then identifies and recommends solution options.

Critical exam distinction:

  • KA2 (Elicitation) = GATHERING information from stakeholders
  • KA3 (RLCM) = MANAGING the lifecycle of requirements (trace, maintain, prioritize, approve)
  • KA4 (Strategy) = STRATEGIC direction (current state, future state, change strategy)
  • KA5 (RADD) = ANALYZING, SPECIFYING, MODELING, VERIFYING, VALIDATING requirements AND defining design options

Key principle: RADD transforms raw elicitation results into well-structured, quality-checked requirements and designs, then identifies the best solution option.

2. THE 6 TASKS — Quick Reference

#TaskPrimary OutputCore Question
1Specify and Model RequirementsRequirements (Specified and Modelled)What exactly do we need?
2Verify RequirementsRequirements (Verified)Are they well-written and correct?
3Validate RequirementsRequirements (Validated)Do they deliver value?
4Define Requirements ArchitectureRequirements ArchitectureHow do requirements fit together?
5Define Design OptionsDesign OptionsWhat solutions could work?
6Analyze Potential Value and Recommend SolutionSolution RecommendationWhich option is best?

Note: KA5 has 6 tasks (the most of any KA). This matches its 30% exam weight.

3. TASK-BY-TASK DEEP DIVE

TASK 1: Specify and Model Requirements

Purpose: Analyze, synthesize, and refine elicitation results into requirements and designs using text, matrices, and diagrams.

Inputs:

  • Elicitation Results (Confirmed) — from KA2
  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)

Output:

  • Requirements (Specified and Modelled)
  • Designs (Specified and Modelled)

Key Elements:

  • Specify: Express requirements clearly in text (use cases, user stories, business rules, acceptance criteria)
  • Model: Represent requirements visually using diagrams, matrices, and other structured formats

Model Categories (MEMORIZE — heavily tested):

CategoryWhat It RepresentsExample Models
People and RolesWho interacts with the systemUse case diagrams, Org models, Stakeholder maps, Roles & permissions matrices
RationaleWhy things are doneBusiness rules, Decision tables, Decision trees
Activity FlowHow things happen (process)Activity diagrams, Process flows, Sequence diagrams, State diagrams, User stories
CapabilityWhat the system/org can doFeature models, Functional decomposition, Scope models
Data and InformationWhat data exists and its structureData models (ERDs), Data dictionaries, Data flow diagrams, Class diagrams

Modelling Notation Types:

  • Matrices: Two-dimensional tables (e.g., RACI chart, traceability matrix)
  • Diagrams: Visual models (e.g., use case diagram, ERD, process flow)
  • Text: Structured narrative (e.g., user stories, business rules, acceptance criteria)

Techniques Used:

  • Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Concept Modelling
  • Data Dictionary
  • Data Flow Diagrams
  • Data Modelling
  • Decision Modelling
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Glossaries
  • Interface Analysis
  • Interaction Modelling
  • Non-Functional Requirements Analysis
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Modelling
  • Prototyping
  • Reviews
  • Roles and Permissions Matrix
  • Scope Modelling
  • Sequence Diagrams
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • State Modelling
  • Use Cases and Scenarios
  • User Stories

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Specifying and modelling are TWO activities within one task. A requirement can be specified (text) without being modelled (visual), and vice versa.
  • "The BA creates a data model to capture entity relationships" → Specify and Model Requirements (Task 1) using the Data Modelling technique.
  • Not all requirements need all model types. The BA selects appropriate models based on stakeholder needs and complexity.
  • User Stories and Use Cases are BOTH specification techniques but serve different contexts (Adaptive vs. Predictive).
  • Prototyping is used here to REFINE requirements, not just to elicit them (it's also used in KA2 for elicitation).

TASK 2: Verify Requirements

Purpose: Ensure that requirements and designs meet QUALITY STANDARDS and are usable for the purpose they serve.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (Specified and Modelled) — from Task 1

Output:

  • Requirements (Verified)

Key Elements — The 9 Quality Characteristics (MEMORIZE ALL 9):

#CharacteristicDefinitionCheck Question
1AtomicSelf-contained; can be understood independently"Can this stand alone without referencing other requirements?"
2CompleteContains enough detail to guide further work"Is anything missing?"
3ConsistentDoes not conflict with other requirements"Does this contradict anything else?"
4ConciseNo extraneous or unnecessary content"Can I say this more briefly without losing meaning?"
5FeasibleReasonable and possible within constraints"Can this be built with our time/budget/technology?"
6UnambiguousOnly one possible interpretation"Could anyone read this differently?"
7TestableCan be verified that it has been fulfilled"Can I write a test for this?"
8PrioritizedRanked relative to other requirements"Do we know how important this is?"
9UnderstandableUses terminology the audience knows"Will developers/users understand this?"

Mnemonic for 9 Characteristics: "A-C-C-C-F-U-T-P-U"

  • Think: "All Characteristics Can Create Fantastic, Useful, Testable, Prioritized Understanding"

Techniques Used:

  • Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria
  • Item Tracking
  • Reviews ← primary technique
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS — The #1 Most Tested Concept in CBAP:

VERIFY vs. VALIDATE — Know this distinction cold:

AspectVERIFY (Task 2)VALIDATE (Task 3)
Question"Is the requirement well-written?""Is the requirement VALUABLE?"
FocusQUALITY of the requirementVALUE of the requirement
Checks9 quality characteristicsAlignment with business needs
Analogy"Did we write the requirement RIGHT?""Did we write the RIGHT requirement?"
WhenAfter specifyingAfter verifying
WhoBA (often with peers)BA with stakeholders
  • "The BA reviews requirements for completeness and consistency" → VERIFY (quality check)
  • "The BA checks if requirements will deliver the expected business value" → VALIDATE (value check)
  • "The requirement says 'the system should be fast'" → FAILS verification (not testable, not unambiguous)
  • A requirement CAN be verified (well-written) but FAIL validation (it doesn't deliver value)

TASK 3: Validate Requirements

Purpose: Ensure requirements and designs align with business requirements and support the delivery of needed VALUE.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (Verified) — from Task 2 (ideally verified first, though iteration is possible)

Output:

  • Requirements (Validated)

Key Elements — The 3 Validation Checks:

CheckQuestionWhat It Means
Necessary"Does this requirement add value?"Every requirement must contribute to the business need
Sufficient"Do ALL requirements together meet the future state objectives?"No gaps in coverage
Stakeholder Agreement"Do stakeholders agree these are the right requirements?"Consensus reached

Techniques Used:

  • Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria ← primary technique
  • Item Tracking
  • Metrics and KPIs
  • Reviews
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Validate checks ALIGNMENT WITH BUSINESS NEEDS — not quality (that's verify).
  • "A requirement is well-written but doesn't contribute to the business goal" → It passes VERIFICATION but FAILS VALIDATION.
  • "The BA discovers a missing requirement that is needed to achieve the future state" → Identified during VALIDATION (the sufficiency check).
  • Validation connects back to KA4 (Strategy Analysis) — you're checking if requirements will achieve the FUTURE STATE.
  • Don't confuse Validate with Approve (KA3 Task 5). Validation = "Is it the right requirement?" Approval = "Are we authorized to proceed?"

TASK 4: Define Requirements Architecture

Purpose: Structure and organize requirements in a way that supports the overall business purpose and is useful to stakeholders.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)

Output:

  • Requirements Architecture

Key Elements:

  • Viewpoints and Views:
  • Viewpoint = a particular PERSPECTIVE for looking at requirements (e.g., business owner's perspective, developer's perspective, tester's perspective)
  • View = the actual REQUIREMENTS seen from that viewpoint
  • Think: Viewpoint = the window you look through; View = what you see through it
  • Requirements structure: Organizing requirements into hierarchies and relationships
  • Abstraction levels: Business → Stakeholder → Solution → Transition
  • Completeness check: Does the architecture cover all aspects of the solution?
  • Relationships: How do different views relate to each other?

Techniques Used:

  • Data Flow Diagrams
  • Data Modelling
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Interaction Modelling
  • Interface Analysis
  • Organization Modelling
  • Process Modelling
  • Scope Modelling

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Requirements Architecture ≠ Solution Architecture. Requirements architecture organizes REQUIREMENTS. Solution architecture organizes the TECHNICAL SOLUTION.
  • Viewpoint vs. View is one of the most tested BABOK v3 definitions:
  • Viewpoint = perspective/framework for looking at requirements
  • View = the actual content seen from that perspective
  • "What does a developer need to see?" → That's the VIEWPOINT (developer perspective). The actual models/diagrams shown → that's the VIEW.
  • Requirements architecture ensures requirements are COHESIVE — they work together as a complete whole.
  • "The BA organizes requirements so that developers see technical specs while business users see process flows" → Define Requirements Architecture (creating different views for different viewpoints).

TASK 5: Define Design Options

Purpose: Identify and describe possible solution approaches that can address the requirements.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Designs (any state)
  • Change Strategy (from KA4)

Output:

  • Design Options

Key Elements:

  • Solution approach: Build, buy, configure, outsource, or combination
  • Design elements:
  • Technology components
  • Process changes
  • Organizational changes
  • Data/information changes
  • Constraints consideration: Budget, time, technology, regulations, organizational limitations
  • Design mapping: Map each design option to the requirements it addresses
  • Improvement opportunities: Where can the solution go beyond minimum requirements to add extra value?

Techniques Used:

  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Capability Analysis
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Collaborative Games
  • Concept Modelling
  • Data Flow Diagrams
  • Data Modelling
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Functional Decomposition
  • Glossaries
  • Interface Analysis
  • Interviews
  • Lessons Learned
  • Mind Mapping
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Modelling
  • Prototyping
  • Roles and Permissions Matrix
  • Scope Modelling
  • Sequence Diagrams
  • State Modelling
  • Use Cases and Scenarios
  • User Stories
  • Vendor Assessment
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Define Design Options (KA5) is MORE DETAILED than Define Change Strategy (KA4). KA4 decides the strategic approach (build vs. buy); KA5 defines the specific options within that approach.
  • "The BA presents 3 vendor products as possible solutions" → Define Design Options (Task 5).
  • Design Options include NON-TECHNOLOGY solutions: process changes, organizational restructuring, policy updates.
  • Each design option should be mapped to the requirements it addresses — this helps with the value analysis in Task 6.

TASK 6: Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution

Purpose: Estimate the potential value of each solution option, compare options, and recommend the best one.

Inputs:

  • Requirements (any state)
  • Design Options (from Task 5)
  • Change Strategy (from KA4)

Output:

  • Solution Recommendation

Key Elements:

  • Value estimation: For each design option, estimate:
  • Benefits (tangible and intangible)
  • Costs (development, maintenance, training, licensing)
  • Risks
  • Time to value
  • Comparison of options: Side-by-side analysis using defined criteria
  • Trade-offs: Every option has advantages and disadvantages
  • Recommendation: Present the best option with clear rationale
  • May recommend a single option
  • May recommend a combination
  • May recommend "do nothing" if no option delivers sufficient value
  • Assumptions and constraints: Document what was assumed in the analysis

Techniques Used:

  • Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria
  • Business Cases
  • Decision Analysis ← primary technique
  • Estimation
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Metrics and KPIs
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Vendor Assessment
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • The BA RECOMMENDS, but does not DECIDE. Stakeholders make the final decision.
  • "Do nothing" is always a valid option. If no solution delivers sufficient value, recommending no change is appropriate.
  • "The BA compares three solutions on cost, benefit, risk, and feasibility" → Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution (Task 6).
  • Don't confuse with KA4 Task 4 (Define Change Strategy). KA4 sets the strategic direction; KA5 Task 6 evaluates specific detailed options.
  • Financial analysis (ROI, NPV, payback) is used HERE at the detailed level, and also in KA4 at the strategic level.

5. VERIFY vs. VALIDATE — THE ULTIMATE COMPARISON

This is the single highest-ROI concept for the CBAP exam. Let me give you every angle.

10. COMMON EXAM QUESTION PATTERNS FOR KA5

Pattern 1: Verify or Validate?

Setup: Scenario describes checking requirements.

Decision rule:

  • Checking QUALITY (well-written, testable, unambiguous) → Verify
  • Checking VALUE (aligns with business goals, delivers benefits) → Validate

Pattern 2: "The requirement says 'the system should be user-friendly'"

Setup: Poorly written requirement.

Correct answer: Fails VERIFICATION — not testable, not unambiguous

What the BA should do: Refine to measurable criteria (e.g., "95% of users can complete checkout in under 3 minutes")

Pattern 3: "Which model should the BA use?"

Setup: Scenario describes a specific information need.

Decision guide:

NeedBest Model
Show who interacts with the systemUse case diagram
Show data structureERD / Data model
Show process stepsActivity diagram / Process flow
Show conditions and outcomesDecision table / Decision tree
Show system boundariesContext diagram / Scope model
Show data movementData flow diagram
Show object statesState diagram
Show message sequencesSequence diagram
Show organizational structureOrg model
Capture rulesBusiness rules catalog

Pattern 4: "The BA needs to organize requirements for different audiences"

Setup: Multiple stakeholders need different views of the same requirements.

Correct answer: Define Requirements Architecture (Task 4) — create different views for different viewpoints.

Common distractor: "Communicate BA Information" (KA2 Task 4) — communication is about SHARING; architecture is about STRUCTURING.

Pattern 5: "The BA presents 3 solution options to the steering committee"

Setup: Comparison of options for a decision.

Correct answer: Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution (Task 6)

Common distractor: "Define Design Options" (Task 5) — defining options is CREATING them; Task 6 is EVALUATING and RECOMMENDING.

Pattern 6: "A requirement passes verification but fails validation"

Setup: Well-written requirement that doesn't deliver value.

Correct answer: The requirement is of high quality but is NOT NECESSARY — it doesn't support the business need.

Action: Remove or modify the requirement, as it doesn't contribute to the future state.

Pattern 7: "The BA discovers during verification that two requirements contradict each other"

Setup: Consistency issue.

Correct answer: The requirements fail the CONSISTENCY check (one of the 9 quality characteristics — VERIFY).

Action: Resolve the conflict, potentially through additional elicitation.

Pattern 8: "Viewpoint vs. View?"

Setup: Definitional question embedded in scenario.

Answer: Viewpoint = the perspective; View = the actual requirements seen from that perspective.

Example: The "developer viewpoint" might include views like data models, sequence diagrams, and technical specifications.

  • VeriFy = Fidelity (quality of writing)
  • ValiDate = Delivers value (alignment with needs)

5-Way Distinction: Confirm → Verify → Validate → Approve → Accept

1. How many tasks does KA5 have?

2. What is the exam weight of KA5?

True — if no option delivers sufficient value

It's well-written but doesn't deliver value (not necessary)

Specify = express in text; Model = represent visually

title: KA5 — Requirements Analysis and Design Definition

content:
CBAP Cheat Sheet — KA6: Solution Evaluation

Exam Weight: ~8% of exam questions — the LIGHTEST knowledge area. Expect roughly 10 scenario-based questions. Don't underestimate it: while few in number, KA6 questions are often the trickiest because they test nuanced distinctions (solution vs. enterprise limitations, performance vs. value).

1. PURPOSE OF THIS KA

This KA defines how the BA evaluates the performance of solutions already in action — prototypes, pilots, or fully operational solutions — and recommends actions to increase the value they deliver.

Critical exam distinction:

  • KA4 (Strategy Analysis) = BEFORE the solution — analyzing needs, defining future state
  • KA5 (RADD) = DURING analysis — specifying and recommending a solution
  • KA6 (Solution Evaluation) = AFTER (or during) deployment — did the solution deliver value?

Key principle: Solution Evaluation is about VALUE REALIZATION. It closes the loop between what was planned (KA4) and what was delivered.

When does KA6 happen?

  • Can start early: evaluating a prototype or pilot
  • During deployment: evaluating incremental releases
  • After go-live: evaluating the operational solution
  • Ongoing: continuous evaluation of value delivery

2. THE 5 TASKS — Quick Reference

#TaskPrimary OutputCore Question
1Measure Solution PerformanceSolution Performance MeasuresHow do we measure if it's working?
2Analyze Performance MeasuresSolution Performance AnalysisIs it actually working?
3Assess Solution LimitationsSolution Limitations (identified)What's wrong INSIDE the solution?
4Assess Enterprise LimitationsEnterprise Limitations (identified)What's wrong OUTSIDE the solution?
5Recommend Actions to Increase Solution ValueSolution Value RecommendationsWhat should we do about it?

3. TASK-BY-TASK DEEP DIVE

TASK 1: Measure Solution Performance

Purpose: Define the performance measures used to evaluate whether the solution is delivering expected value, and collect the measurement data.

Inputs:

  • Solution Performance Measures (existing, if any)
  • Implemented Solution (external — the actual deployed solution)

Output:

  • Solution Performance Measures

Key Elements:

  • Define what to measure: Align measures with the business goals and objectives from KA4 (future state)
  • Types of measures:
Measure TypeWhat It TracksExample
EffectivenessDoes the solution achieve its purpose?"Order processing errors reduced by 80%"
EfficiencyDoes it use resources well?"Processing time reduced from 5 min to 1 min"
Stakeholder satisfactionAre users/customers happy?"NPS score of 75; user satisfaction 4.5/5"
FinancialFinancial returns"ROI of 150%; cost savings of €500K/year"
ComplianceDoes it meet regulatory requirements?"100% audit compliance achieved"
  • Establish baselines: Measure current performance BEFORE the solution (or use KA4 current state data)
  • Data collection: Define how, when, and by whom measurements are taken

Techniques Used:

  • Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria
  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Cases
  • Data Mining
  • Data Modelling
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Metrics and KPIs ← primary technique
  • Non-Functional Requirements Analysis
  • Observation
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Prototyping
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Use Cases and Scenarios
  • User Stories
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Measuring performance is about DEFINING MEASURES and COLLECTING DATA, not analyzing it (that's Task 2).
  • "The BA defines KPIs for the new system" → Measure Solution Performance (Task 1).
  • Performance measures should trace back to the business goals defined in KA4 (Define Future State). If they don't, the measures are meaningless.
  • Don't confuse with KA1 Task 5 (Identify BA Performance Improvements) — KA1 evaluates the BA PROCESS; KA6 evaluates the SOLUTION.
  • The measures can be defined BEFORE the solution is implemented — so this task can start early.

TASK 2: Analyze Performance Measures

Purpose: Analyze the collected performance data to understand whether the solution is delivering expected value.

Inputs:

  • Solution Performance Measures (from Task 1)
  • Implemented Solution (external)

Output:

  • Solution Performance Analysis

Key Elements:

  • Compare actual vs. expected: Did the solution meet the targets defined in KA4?
  • Identify variances: Where are the gaps between expected and actual performance?
  • Trend analysis: Is performance improving, stable, or declining over time?
  • Root cause investigation: If performance is below target, begin understanding why (detailed root cause happens in Tasks 3 & 4)
  • Stakeholder collaboration: Work with stakeholders to interpret the data and agree on findings

Techniques Used:

  • Business Cases
  • Data Mining
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Metrics and KPIs
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Analyze ≠ Measure. Task 1 DEFINES metrics and COLLECTS data. Task 2 INTERPRETS the data.
  • "The BA discovers the new system reduced processing time by only 10% instead of the expected 40%" → Analyze Performance Measures (Task 2) — identifying the variance.
  • The output (Solution Performance Analysis) feeds into BOTH Task 3 (Solution Limitations) and Task 4 (Enterprise Limitations).
  • "The data shows the solution is performing well" → Even positive results are analyzed here. Task 2 isn't only for bad news.

TASK 3: Assess Solution Limitations

Purpose: Identify root causes of performance gaps that are INTERNAL to the solution.

Inputs:

  • Solution Performance Analysis (from Task 2)
  • Implemented Solution (external)

Output:

  • Solution Limitations (identified and documented)

Key Elements:

  • Internal root causes: Problems WITHIN the solution itself
  • Types of solution limitations:
Limitation TypeDescriptionExample
Defects/BugsThe solution doesn't work as designed"Search returns incorrect results for special characters"
Performance issuesThe solution is too slow, unreliable"Page load time exceeds 10 seconds at peak"
Missing functionalityRequired features were not built"Report export feature was descoped"
Design flawsArchitecture/design doesn't support the need"System can't handle more than 100 concurrent users"
Data qualityData within the solution is inaccurate"Customer addresses imported with errors"
Usability issuesSolution is hard to use"5-click process for a task that should take 2"
  • Root cause analysis: Dig into WHY the limitation exists
  • Impact assessment: How much does this limitation reduce value delivery?

Techniques Used:

  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Data Mining
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Observation
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Root Cause Analysis ← primary technique
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS — The #1 KA6 Distinction:

Solution Limitations vs. Enterprise Limitations:

DimensionSolution Limitations (Task 3)Enterprise Limitations (Task 4)
ScopeINTERNAL to the solutionEXTERNAL to the solution
Root causeWithin the solution itselfIn the organization around the solution
ExamplesBugs, performance issues, missing featuresInadequate training, poor processes, cultural resistance
FixChange the solution (patch, upgrade, redesign)Change the enterprise (train, reorganize, update processes)
AnalogyThe car has a flat tireThe road has potholes
  • "The system crashes when processing large files" → Solution Limitation (bug/design flaw inside the solution).
  • "Users aren't using the new system because they weren't trained" → Enterprise Limitation (training gap outside the solution).
  • These two tasks are often performed CONCURRENTLY — the exam may ask which applies to a specific scenario.

TASK 4: Assess Enterprise Limitations

Purpose: Identify root causes of performance gaps that are EXTERNAL to the solution — factors in the enterprise that prevent full value realization.

Inputs:

  • Solution Performance Analysis (from Task 2)
  • Implemented Solution (external)

Output:

  • Enterprise Limitations (identified and documented)

Key Elements:

  • External root causes: Problems in the ORGANIZATION, not the solution
  • Types of enterprise limitations:
Limitation TypeDescriptionExample
Stakeholder/PeopleUsers unable or unwilling to use the solution"Staff reverting to old manual processes"
Training gapsInadequate training on the new solution"Only 30% of users completed training"
Process gapsBusiness processes not updated for the new solution"Approval workflow still requires paper forms"
Organizational structureOrg structure doesn't support the solution"No team assigned to maintain the new system"
Culture/ResistanceOrganizational resistance to change"Middle management undermining adoption"
Policy/ComplianceOutdated policies conflict with the solution"Policy requires manual signature on documents the system digitized"
InfrastructureSupporting infrastructure inadequate"Network bandwidth insufficient for cloud solution"
SkillsWorkforce lacks required skills"No staff trained in the new technology"
  • Operational assessment: Evaluate the enterprise's ability to adapt to and use the solution effectively
  • Stakeholder impact analysis: How are different stakeholder groups affected?
  • Broad perspective: BABOK advises looking widely — the limitation might not be obvious

Techniques Used:

  • Benchmarking and Market Analysis
  • Business Rules Analysis
  • Data Mining
  • Decision Analysis
  • Document Analysis
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Observation
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • Enterprise limitations are about the ENVIRONMENT, not the solution. Even a perfect solution can fail if the enterprise isn't ready.
  • "Users are reverting to the old manual process despite the new system working correctly" → Enterprise Limitation (people/culture issue, NOT a solution defect).
  • "The new system works perfectly in testing but fails in production due to network issues" → Enterprise Limitation (infrastructure outside the solution).
  • The Operational Assessment is a key element of this task — it evaluates the org's readiness to use the solution.
  • Stakeholder Impact Analysis belongs HERE in Task 4 — assessing how stakeholders are affected by or affecting the solution's value.

TASK 5: Recommend Actions to Increase Solution Value

Purpose: Recommend actions to resolve identified limitations and increase the value the solution delivers.

Inputs:

  • Solution Limitations (from Task 3)
  • Enterprise Limitations (from Task 4)
  • Solution Performance Analysis (from Task 2)

Output:

  • Solution Value Recommendations

Key Elements:

  • Action types:
ActionWhen to UseExample
Do nothingLimitation is minor; cost of fixing > impact"Accept the cosmetic UI issue"
Modify the solutionSolution limitation with viable fix"Patch the performance bug"
Modify the enterpriseEnterprise limitation requires org change"Provide additional training"
Replace the solutionSolution is fundamentally inadequate"Migrate to new platform"
Retire the solutionSolution no longer delivers value"Decommission the legacy system"
Enhance the solutionSolution works but could deliver more value"Add reporting dashboard"
  • Cost-benefit analysis: For each recommendation, assess cost vs. expected value gain
  • Prioritization: Rank recommendations by impact and feasibility
  • Stakeholder agreement: Ensure stakeholders support the recommendations
  • Feedback loop: Recommendations may trigger new Strategy Analysis (KA4) or new requirements (KA5)

Techniques Used:

  • Business Cases
  • Decision Analysis ← primary technique
  • Estimation
  • Financial Analysis
  • Focus Groups
  • Interviews
  • Item Tracking
  • Lessons Learned
  • Metrics and KPIs
  • Organizational Modelling
  • Process Analysis
  • Process Modelling
  • Risk Analysis and Management
  • Root Cause Analysis
  • Survey or Questionnaire
  • Workshops

⚠️ EXAM TRAPS:

  • "Retire the solution" and "Do nothing" are VALID recommendations. Don't assume the answer always involves fixing something.
  • "Replace the solution" triggers a NEW cycle of Strategy Analysis (KA4) — it's essentially starting over.
  • The BA RECOMMENDS; stakeholders DECIDE. Same rule as KA5.
  • "The BA determines the cost of fixing a bug exceeds the value lost due to the bug" → Recommend "Do nothing" or "Accept."
  • Recommendations can be for BOTH solution changes (fix/enhance/replace) AND enterprise changes (train/reorganize/update policies).
  • This task closes the feedback loop — the outputs may feed back into KA1 (new BA planning), KA4 (new strategy), or KA5 (new requirements).

4. INPUTS AND OUTPUTS — MASTER MAP


Implemented Solution (external)
        │
        ├──→ Measure Solution Performance ──→ Solution Performance Measures
        │                                          │
        │                                          ↓
        ├──→ Analyze Performance Measures ──→ Solution Performance Analysis
        │                                          │
        │                              ┌───────────┴───────────┐
        │                              ↓                       ↓
        ├──→ Assess Solution Limitations  Assess Enterprise Limitations
        │            │                              │
        │            ↓                              ↓
        │    Solution Limitations          Enterprise Limitations
        │            │                              │
        │            └──────────┬───────────────────┘
        │                       ↓
        └──→ Recommend Actions to Increase Solution Value
                                │
                                ↓
                    Solution Value Recommendations
                                │
                    ┌───────────┼───────────┐
                    ↓           ↓           ↓
              KA4 (new      KA5 (new    KA1 (new
              strategy)     requirements) planning)
                    FEEDBACK LOOP

Key insight: KA6 creates a FEEDBACK LOOP. Its recommendations can trigger new work in any other KA, making business analysis a continuous cycle, not a linear process.

5. SOLUTION LIMITATIONS vs. ENTERPRISE LIMITATIONS — THE ULTIMATE COMPARISON

This is the single most tested distinction in KA6.

Question to AskIf YES →If YES →
"Is the problem in the software/system itself?"Solution Limitation
"Would fixing the code/configuration resolve it?"Solution Limitation
"Is the problem with people, processes, or organization?"Enterprise Limitation
"Does the solution work in testing but fail in the real environment?"Enterprise Limitation

Scenario Decision Guide:

ScenarioAnswerWhy
System crashes under heavy loadSolution LimitationDesign/performance flaw in the system
Users don't use the new reporting featureEnterprise LimitationTraining/awareness/adoption issue
Data migration introduced errorsSolution LimitationData quality issue within the solution
Help desk can't support the new systemEnterprise LimitationOrganizational capability gap
The system correctly implements requirements, but user satisfaction is lowEnterprise LimitationLikely process/expectation mismatch outside the solution
The search feature returns wrong resultsSolution LimitationBug/defect in the solution
Network bandwidth is too low for the cloud solutionEnterprise LimitationInfrastructure gap outside the solution
The approval workflow was not redesigned for the new systemEnterprise LimitationProcess gap in the organization

6. VALUE REALIZATION — The Central Concept

KA6 is fundamentally about VALUE. Understand this flow:


PLANNED VALUE                    ACTUAL VALUE
(from KA4 Future State)          (measured in KA6)
         │                              │
         └──── VALUE GAP = ─────────────┘
                    │
            ┌───────┴───────┐
            ↓               ↓
    Solution          Enterprise
    Limitations       Limitations
            │               │
            └───────┬───────┘
                    ↓
            Recommendations
            to close the gap

Potential Value vs. Actual Value:

  • Potential Value = what the solution COULD deliver (estimated in KA4/KA5)
  • Actual Value = what the solution IS delivering (measured in KA6)
  • Value Gap = Potential - Actual = what's being lost due to limitations
