Memory tricks:

  • Universal across all 5 tasks: Financial Analysis, Focus Groups, Interviews, Item Tracking, Process Analysis, Process Modelling, Survey/Questionnaire, Workshops — "F-F-I-I-P-P-S-W"
  • Root Cause Analysis appears in Tasks 2, 3, 4, and 5 — because finding and addressing root causes is central to evaluation
  • Task 1 (Measure) has the most techniques (20) — because defining measures requires looking at many dimensions
  • Organizational Modelling only appears in Tasks 4 and 5 — because it's about the ENTERPRISE, not the solution
  • Prototyping, Use Cases, User Stories only appear in Task 1 — because they help DEFINE what to measure

8. COMMON EXAM QUESTION PATTERNS FOR KA6

Pattern 1: "Solution Limitation or Enterprise Limitation?"

Setup: Performance gap described; must identify root cause type.

Decision rule:

  • Problem IN the system (bugs, design, data) → Solution Limitation
  • Problem AROUND the system (people, process, org) → Enterprise Limitation

Pattern 2: "The solution is live but not delivering expected value"

Setup: Post-deployment value gap.

Correct answer sequence:

  • Analyze Performance Measures (Task 2) — understand the gap
  • Assess Solution Limitations (Task 3) AND Assess Enterprise Limitations (Task 4) — find root causes
  • Recommend Actions (Task 5) — propose fixes

Common distractor: "Go back to requirements" — wrong; evaluate first, THEN decide if new requirements are needed.

Pattern 3: "The BA needs to define how to measure the solution's success"

Setup: Pre- or post-deployment, need KPIs.

Correct answer: Measure Solution Performance (Task 1)

Key: Measures should align with the business goals from KA4.

Common distractor: "Validate Requirements" (KA5 Task 3) — validation checks if requirements deliver value; measuring performance checks if the SOLUTION delivers value.

Pattern 4: "The BA recommends retiring the solution"

Setup: Solution no longer delivers value.

Correct answer: Recommend Actions to Increase Solution Value (Task 5)

Key: "Retire" is a valid recommendation. Not every solution should be kept.

Common distractor: "This can't be right because it's about increasing value" — retiring a value-destroying solution DOES increase overall value.

Pattern 5: "Users were not trained on the new system"

Setup: Adoption problem.

Correct answer: Enterprise Limitation (Task 4) — training gap is EXTERNAL to the solution.

Action: Recommend training (Task 5).

Common distractor: "Solution Limitation" — the solution works; the problem is with the organization.

Pattern 6: "Distinguish KA6 from KA1 Task 5"

Setup: Performance assessment question.

Decision rule:

  • Evaluating the BA PROCESS performance → KA1 Task 5 (Identify BA Performance Improvements)
  • Evaluating the SOLUTION performance → KA6 (Solution Evaluation)

Pattern 7: "Distinguish KA6 from KA5 Task 3"

Setup: Validation vs. evaluation question.

Decision rule:

  • Checking if REQUIREMENTS deliver value (before solution is built) → KA5 Task 3 (Validate)
  • Checking if the SOLUTION delivers value (after it's deployed) → KA6 (Solution Evaluation)

Pattern 8: "The recommendation triggers new strategy work"

Setup: Evaluation reveals the solution is fundamentally inadequate.

Correct answer: Recommend replacing the solution (Task 5), which triggers new KA4 (Strategy Analysis).

Key insight: KA6 creates a FEEDBACK LOOP — the cycle of business analysis is continuous.

9. KEY DEFINITIONS TO MEMORIZE

TermDefinitionDon't Confuse With
Solution Performance MeasureA metric used to evaluate whether the solution delivers valueRequirement attribute (metadata about a requirement)
Solution Performance AnalysisInterpretation of measured data to assess value deliveryRisk analysis (assessing what COULD happen; performance analysis assesses what IS happening)
Solution LimitationAn internal factor within the solution that reduces valueEnterprise limitation (external factor)
Enterprise LimitationAn external factor around the solution that reduces valueSolution limitation (internal factor)
Value GapDifference between planned and actual value deliveredRequirement gap (missing requirement)
Operational AssessmentEvaluation of the org's ability to use the solution effectivelyRequirements assessment (checking quality/value of requirements)
Stakeholder Impact AnalysisAssessment of how stakeholders are affected by the solutionStakeholder analysis (identifying stakeholder characteristics — KA1)

10. CROSS-KA CONNECTIONS (Exam Favorites)

KA6 ElementConnects ToHow
Performance MeasuresKA4 (Strategy — Future State)Measures should trace to business goals defined in KA4
Performance AnalysisKA4 (Strategy — Current State)Compares actual results to the planned future state
Solution LimitationsKA5 (RADD)May trigger new/modified requirements
Enterprise LimitationsKA4 (Strategy)May trigger new change strategy
RecommendationsKA1 (Planning)May trigger new BA planning for a new initiative
RecommendationsKA3 (RLCM)May trigger requirement changes
Solution Evaluation overallKA1 Task 5 (BA Performance)KA6 evaluates the SOLUTION; KA1 T5 evaluates the BA PROCESS

The Full BA Cycle:


KA4 (Strategy) → KA1 (Plan) → KA2 (Elicit) → KA5 (Analyze) → KA3 (Manage) → Implementation → KA6 (Evaluate) → back to KA4

11. PREDICTIVE vs. ADAPTIVE — Impact on KA6

AspectPredictiveAdaptive
When evaluatedPost-deployment, at milestonesPer iteration, continuously
Measures definedUpfront with business caseEvolve with product backlog
Performance analysisFormal reports, variance analysisSprint reviews, demos, retrospectives
Solution limitationsPost-deployment defect trackingIdentified during iteration reviews
Enterprise limitationsAssessed during change managementAssessed continuously
RecommendationsFormal change requestsBacklog items for next iteration
Feedback loopMilestone-basedContinuous

12. SOLUTION EVALUATION TIMING

KA6 is NOT only a post-project activity. Know when it applies:

Solution StateKA6 Applies?Example
PrototypeYes"Evaluate the prototype with users to assess if the design concept works"
Pilot/BetaYes"Measure adoption rates during the pilot rollout"
Incremental ReleaseYes"Evaluate each sprint's deliverable against acceptance criteria"
Full DeploymentYes"Assess whether the full solution meets business objectives"
Operational (ongoing)Yes"Continuously monitor solution performance over time"
End of LifeYes"Evaluate whether the solution should be retired"

13. MNEMONICS AND MEMORY AIDS

5 Tasks in Order: "M-A-S-E-R" (Measure, Analyze, Solution limitations, Enterprise limitations, Recommend)

  • Think: "MASER" — like a laser, KA6 focuses precisely on value

Solution vs. Enterprise Limitations:

  • Solution = System (inside the box)
  • Enterprise = Environment (outside the box)

5 Recommendation Actions: "D-M-M-R-R-E" (Do nothing, Modify solution, Modify enterprise, Replace, Retire, Enhance)

  • Think: "Don't Miss Making the Right Recommendation Ever"

KA6 vs. KA1 Task 5:

  • KA6 = evaluates the Solution (6 and S look similar)
  • KA1 = evaluates the BA Process (1 and P — Process is Priority #1)

The Feedback Loop: KA6 → KA4 → KA1 → KA2 → KA5 → KA3 → KA6 → ...

  • Business analysis NEVER truly ends. It's a continuous cycle of delivering and evaluating value.

14. RAPID-FIRE SELF-TEST (20 Questions)

1. What is the exam weight of KA6?

~8% (the lightest)

2. Name the 5 tasks in KA6.

Measure Solution Performance, Analyze Performance Measures, Assess Solution Limitations, Assess Enterprise Limitations, Recommend Actions to Increase Solution Value

3. A system bug causes incorrect reports. Solution or enterprise limitation?

Solution Limitation (defect inside the system)

4. Users weren't trained on the new system. Solution or enterprise limitation?

Enterprise Limitation (training gap outside the system)

5. What is the difference between KA6 and KA1 Task 5?

KA6 evaluates the SOLUTION; KA1 Task 5 evaluates the BA PROCESS

6. What is the difference between KA6 and KA5 Task 3 (Validate)?

KA5 T3 checks if REQUIREMENTS deliver value (before build); KA6 checks if the SOLUTION delivers value (after deployment)

7. Is "retire the solution" a valid recommendation?

Yes — if the solution no longer delivers value

8. Is "do nothing" a valid recommendation?

Yes — if the cost of fixing exceeds the impact

9. Where should performance measures trace back to?

Business goals and objectives defined in KA4 (Future State)

10. The network is too slow for the cloud solution. Solution or enterprise limitation?

Enterprise Limitation (infrastructure gap outside the solution)

11. The system can't handle more than 100 concurrent users. Solution or enterprise limitation?

Solution Limitation (design flaw inside the system)

12. Which task DEFINES metrics? Which task INTERPRETS data?

Task 1 defines; Task 2 interprets

13. Can KA6 be performed on a prototype?

Yes — Solution Evaluation applies to prototypes, pilots, and fully deployed solutions

14. What is an Operational Assessment?

Evaluation of the organization's ability to adapt to and use the solution effectively (part of Task 4)

15. A recommendation to replace the solution triggers which KA?

KA4 (Strategy Analysis) — starting a new strategy cycle

16. What is the Value Gap?

The difference between planned (potential) value and actual value delivered

17. Staff are reverting to old manual processes despite the new system working. Which task?

Assess Enterprise Limitations (Task 4) — adoption/culture issue

18. Name 3 types of performance measures.

Effectiveness, Efficiency, Stakeholder satisfaction, Financial, Compliance (any 3)

19. Root Cause Analysis appears in which KA6 tasks?

Tasks 2, 3, 4, and 5

20. Does KA6 create a feedback loop?

Yes — recommendations feed back into KA4, KA5, KA1, and KA3

15. EXAM DAY QUICK REFERENCE

When you see these keywords, think this task:

Keywords→ Task
KPIs, metrics, baseline, measure, define criteria, data collectionMeasure Solution Performance
analyze data, variance, actual vs. expected, trend, interpretAnalyze Performance Measures
bug, defect, design flaw, system issue, internal problem, performance issueAssess Solution Limitations
training, adoption, culture, process gap, organizational, infrastructure, externalAssess Enterprise Limitations
recommend, retire, replace, enhance, do nothing, increase value, action planRecommend Actions

The "Inside or Outside?" Rule:

  • Problem INSIDE the solution → Solution Limitation
  • Problem OUTSIDE the solution → Enterprise Limitation

The KA6 Flow:

  • Measure — define what success looks like and collect data
  • Analyze — compare actual to expected; identify gaps
  • Assess — find root causes (solution AND/OR enterprise)
  • Recommend — propose actions to close the value gap

The "Which KA?" Disambiguation:

  • Evaluating BA PROCESS → KA1 Task 5
  • Checking if REQUIREMENTS are well-written → KA5 Task 2 (Verify)
  • Checking if REQUIREMENTS deliver value → KA5 Task 3 (Validate)
  • Checking if the SOLUTION delivers value → KA6
  • Planning how to do BA work → KA1

16. THE COMPLETE CBAP KA MAP — All 6 Knowledge Areas

Now that you've covered all 6 KAs, here's the master view:

KANameTasksExam WeightCore Focus
KA1BA Planning & Monitoring5~16%HOW to do BA work
KA2Elicitation & Collaboration5~20%GATHERING information
KA3Requirements Life Cycle Management5~16%MANAGING requirements
KA4Strategy Analysis4~15%WHY change is needed
KA5Requirements Analysis & Design Definition6~30%WHAT to build
KA6Solution Evaluation5~8%DID it deliver value
Total30 tasks100%

The BA Lifecycle Circle:


    KA4 (WHY?) ──→ KA1 (HOW?) ──→ KA2 (GATHER) ──→ KA5 (WHAT?)
         ↑                                                │
         │                                                ↓
    KA6 (DID IT?) ←────── Implementation ←────── KA3 (MANAGE)

CBAP Cheat Sheet — Chapter 9: Underlying Competencies

Exam Weight: ~10-15% of questions test competencies either directly or embedded within KA scenarios.

Chapter 9 describes the behaviours, characteristics, knowledge, and personal qualities that support the practice of business analysis.

1. Overview — The 6 Underlying Competency Areas

#Competency AreaFocus
1Analytical Thinking and Problem SolvingHOW you think — breaking down problems, evaluating options
2Behavioural CharacteristicsWHO you are — ethics, trustworthiness, personal accountability
3Business KnowledgeWHAT you know about the business — industry, organization, solutions, methodology
4Communication SkillsHOW you share — verbal, non-verbal, written, listening
5Interaction SkillsHOW you work with others — facilitation, leadership, negotiation, teamwork
6Tools and TechnologyWHAT tools you use — office, BA-specific, communication tools

Mnemonic: A-B-B-C-I-T ("A Big Business Cat Is Tough")

2. Competency 1 — Analytical Thinking and Problem Solving

Sub-Competencies:

Sub-CompetencyDescription
Creative ThinkingGenerating new ideas, exploring novel approaches, thinking outside conventional boundaries
Decision MakingMaking informed decisions based on available information, considering risks and trade-offs
LearningQuickly absorbing new information, adapting to new domains and technologies
Problem SolvingIdentifying root causes, developing and evaluating options, recommending solutions
Systems ThinkingUnderstanding how parts of a system interrelate and how systems work over time within the context of larger systems
Conceptual ThinkingFinding connections between disparate concepts, thinking abstractly
Visual ThinkingUsing visual models and diagrams to understand and communicate complex information

Key Exam Points:

  • Systems Thinking is the MOST tested sub-competency — understanding interconnections, feedback loops, and unintended consequences
  • Creative Thinking ≠ brainstorming — it's a broader ability to generate novel approaches
  • Decision Making involves weighing trade-offs, NOT just choosing the first acceptable option
  • The BA must understand the WHOLE system, not just isolated parts (Systems Thinking)

3. Competency 2 — Behavioural Characteristics

Sub-Competencies:

Sub-CompetencyDescription
EthicsActing with integrity, honesty, and fairness; avoiding conflicts of interest
Personal AccountabilityTaking ownership of work, decisions, and mistakes
TrustworthinessBeing reliable, consistent, and dependable; keeping commitments
Organization and Time ManagementManaging workload, prioritizing tasks, meeting deadlines
AdaptabilityAdjusting approach when circumstances change; being flexible

Key Exam Points:

  • Ethics is frequently tested — the BA must be honest even when it's uncomfortable
  • If a scenario describes a conflict of interest, the answer is ALWAYS to disclose it
  • Personal Accountability = the BA owns their work and doesn't blame others
  • Trustworthiness is built over time through consistent, reliable behavior
  • Adaptability is especially important in Agile contexts

4. Competency 3 — Business Knowledge

Sub-Competencies:

Sub-CompetencyDescription
Business AcumenUnderstanding how businesses operate — revenue models, value chains, competitive dynamics
Industry KnowledgeKnowing the specific industry (healthcare, finance, retail, etc.) — trends, regulations, competitors
Organization KnowledgeUnderstanding the specific organization — culture, structure, strategy, politics, informal networks
Solution KnowledgeUnderstanding the solution landscape — existing systems, technologies, and how they interact
Methodology KnowledgeUnderstanding project methodologies (Agile, Waterfall, Lean, SAFe) and how BA practices adapt to each

Key Exam Points:

  • Business Acumen is about understanding the "big picture" — not just requirements but how the business creates value
  • Organization Knowledge includes INFORMAL networks and politics (not just the org chart)
  • Methodology Knowledge — the BA must know how to adapt their approach to different methodologies
  • A BA with strong Business Knowledge can ask better questions and provide more valuable analysis

5. Competency 4 — Communication Skills

Sub-Competencies:

Sub-CompetencyDescription
Verbal CommunicationSpeaking clearly, adjusting language for the audience, presenting effectively
Non-Verbal CommunicationBody language, tone of voice, facial expressions — reading and projecting
Written CommunicationProducing clear, concise, audience-appropriate documents
ListeningActive listening — hearing what's said AND what's not said, asking clarifying questions

Key Exam Points:

  • Listening is the MOST important communication sub-competency for a BA
  • Active Listening = hearing content + observing non-verbal cues + asking clarifying questions + reflecting back
  • The BA must tailor communication to the AUDIENCE — executives get summaries, developers get details
  • Non-verbal communication — the BA should be aware of body language cues (crossed arms = resistance, eye contact = engagement)
  • Written communication must be clear, concise, and unambiguous — directly linked to KA5 verification quality characteristics

6. Competency 5 — Interaction Skills

Sub-Competencies:

Sub-CompetencyDescription
FacilitationGuiding groups to productive outcomes without directing content
Leadership and InfluencingMotivating and inspiring others; influencing without authority
TeamworkWorking collaboratively, contributing to group goals, supporting team members
Negotiation and Conflict ResolutionFinding mutually acceptable solutions, mediating disagreements
TeachingHelping others understand BA concepts, coaching stakeholders

Key Exam Points:

  • Facilitation — the BA guides the PROCESS, not the CONTENT. The BA is NEUTRAL
  • Leadership and Influencing — the BA often has NO formal authority but must influence outcomes
  • Negotiation is about finding WIN-WIN solutions, NOT about the BA getting their way
  • Conflict Resolution approaches (from BABOK perspective):
  • Collaborate (win-win) — preferred
  • Compromise (give and take) — acceptable
  • Accommodate (give in) — situational
  • Force (push through) — last resort
  • Avoid (withdraw) — sometimes appropriate temporarily
  • The BA TEACHES stakeholders — not just elicits FROM them

7. Competency 6 — Tools and Technology

Sub-Competencies:

Sub-CompetencyDescription
Office Productivity ToolsWord processing, spreadsheets, presentations, email
BA-Specific ToolsRequirements management tools (Jira, DOORS, Azure DevOps), modelling tools (Visio, Enterprise Architect), prototyping tools
Communication TechnologyCollaboration platforms, video conferencing, wikis, shared workspaces

Key Exam Points:

  • This competency is the LEAST tested on the exam
  • The key concept: the BA should use appropriate tools for the context — not every project needs a heavyweight requirements management tool
  • Tool selection should align with the BA Approach (KA1 Task 1) and Information Management Approach (KA1 Task 4)

8. Cross-Competency Exam Traps

TrapCorrect Answer
"The BA should decide for the stakeholders"NO — the BA facilitates decisions; stakeholders decide
"The BA should avoid conflict"NO — the BA should manage conflict constructively
"The BA should focus only on requirements"NO — the BA needs business knowledge to provide context
"The BA should use the same tools for every project"NO — tools should be tailored to context
"Listening means waiting for your turn to speak"NO — active listening involves understanding, reflecting, and clarifying
"The BA should always agree with stakeholders"NO — the BA should provide honest, evidence-based feedback
"Ethics only applies to formal situations"NO — ethical behavior applies always, including informal conversations

9. How Competencies Map to Knowledge Areas

CompetencyMost Relevant KAs
Analytical ThinkingKA4 (Strategy), KA5 (RADD), KA6 (Evaluation)
Behavioural CharacteristicsALL KAs — foundational
Business KnowledgeKA4 (Strategy), KA6 (Evaluation)
Communication SkillsKA2 (Elicitation), KA5 (Communicate)
Interaction SkillsKA2 (Collaboration), KA1 (Stakeholder Engagement)
Tools and TechnologyKA1 (Info Management), KA5 (Modelling)

10. Quick-Fire Summary

  • 6 competency areas, each with multiple sub-competencies
  • Analytical Thinking — the BA thinks critically, solves problems, sees the whole system
  • Behavioural Characteristics — the BA is ethical, accountable, trustworthy, adaptable
  • Business Knowledge — the BA understands the business, industry, organization, solutions, and methodology
  • Communication — the BA listens actively, writes clearly, speaks appropriately, reads body language
  • Interaction Skills — the BA facilitates, leads without authority, negotiates, resolves conflicts, teaches
  • Tools and Technology — the BA uses appropriate tools for the context
  • Systems Thinking and Ethics are the two most frequently tested sub-competencies
  • The BA FACILITATES but does NOT DECIDE for stakeholders
  • Conflict resolution preference: Collaborate > Compromise > Accommodate > Force > Avoid

Sources: Based on IIBA BABOK Guide v3 (Chapter 9) concepts. Content rephrased for compliance with licensing restrictions.

47Use Cases and ScenariosDescribe system interactions step-by-stepKA3, KA5
48User StoriesLightweight requirements in "As a... I want... So that..." formatKA3, KA5
49Vendor AssessmentEvaluate vendor products/servicesKA5
50WorkshopsFacilitated group sessions to produce deliverablesKA1–KA6 (widely used)

2. Tier 1 — Most Heavily Tested Techniques (Know These Cold)

Interviews (Technique 25)

  • Purpose: Gather detailed information from individuals or small groups
  • Types: Structured (fixed questions), Semi-structured (guided with flexibility), Unstructured (open conversation)
  • Elicitation type: Collaborative
  • Used in: ALL KAs — the most universally applicable technique
  • Exam trap: Interviews are Collaborative, not Research

Workshops (Technique 50)

  • Purpose: Facilitated group sessions that produce deliverables and build consensus
  • Key difference from Focus Groups: Workshops PRODUCE deliverables; Focus Groups GATHER reactions
  • Used in: ALL KAs — second most universal technique
  • Exam trap: The BA facilitates (neutral on content) — does NOT direct conclusions

Document Analysis (Technique 18)

  • Purpose: Study existing documents to extract information
  • Elicitation type: Research (no stakeholder interaction needed)
  • Used in: KA1 (planning), KA2 (elicitation)
  • Exam trap: Document Analysis is Research type, NOT Collaborative

Observation (Technique 31)

  • Purpose: Watch people perform work to understand actual practices including undocumented workarounds
  • Elicitation type: Experiment (creates new knowledge)
  • Risk: Hawthorne effect — people change behaviour when observed
  • Exam trap: Observation is an Experiment, NOT Collaborative or Research

Brainstorming (Technique 5)

  • Purpose: Generate many ideas quickly without judgment
  • Key rule: Defer judgment — quantity over quality initially
  • Used in: Widely across KA1-KA5
  • Exam trap: During brainstorming, criticism must be deferred

Prototyping (Technique 36)

  • Purpose: Create mockups to discover/refine requirements
  • Elicitation type: Experiment (creates new knowledge users can't articulate verbally)
  • Risk: Can set unrealistic expectations if users confuse prototype with final product
  • Types: Low-fidelity (paper sketches), High-fidelity (interactive mockups)
  • Exam trap: Prototyping is an Experiment type, not Collaborative

3. Tier 2 — Frequently Tested Techniques

Decision Analysis (Technique 16)

  • Purpose: Evaluate options against weighted criteria to make informed decisions
  • Used in: KA3 (prioritize, approve), KA4 (change strategy), KA5 (design options, recommend), KA6 (recommend actions)
  • Exam tip: Whenever the exam asks about "evaluating options" or "comparing alternatives," Decision Analysis is usually the answer

MoSCoW Analysis (part of Prioritization — Technique 33)

  • Categories: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have (this time)
  • Key point: "Won't Have" means NOT THIS TIME — deferred, not cancelled
  • Used in: KA3 (Prioritize Requirements)

SWOT Analysis (Technique 46)

  • Categories: Strengths (internal+), Weaknesses (internal-), Opportunities (external+), Threats (external-)
  • Used in: KA4 (Tasks 1, 2, 4 — NOT Task 3)
  • Exam trap: S/W are INTERNAL factors; O/T are EXTERNAL factors

Root Cause Analysis (Technique 40)

  • Purpose: Find underlying causes (not just symptoms)
  • Common methods: 5 Whys, Fishbone/Ishikawa diagram
  • Used in: KA1 (performance improvements), KA4 (current state, risks), KA6 (limitation assessment)

Business Rules Analysis (Technique 9)

  • Purpose: Capture conditional business logic and decision rules
  • Output: Business rules catalog, decision tables, decision trees
  • Used in: KA3 (trace), KA5 (specify)
  • Exam tip: When the scenario describes "IF-THEN" conditional logic, Business Rules Analysis is usually the answer

Use Cases and Scenarios (Technique 47)

  • Purpose: Describe system interactions step-by-step (actors, flows, conditions)
  • Components: Actor, Preconditions, Main Flow, Alternative Flows, Exception Flows, Postconditions
  • Used in: KA3 (maintain), KA5 (specify)
  • Exam tip: Use Cases are for PREDICTIVE environments; User Stories (Technique 48) for ADAPTIVE

User Stories (Technique 48)

  • Format: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]"
  • Companion: Acceptance criteria define WHEN the story is "done"
  • Used in: KA3 (maintain), KA5 (specify)
  • Exam tip: User Stories are lightweight and Agile-native

Financial Analysis (Technique 20)

  • Key calculations:
  • ROI = (Net Benefit / Cost) × 100%
  • NPV = Present value of future cash flows minus investment
  • Payback Period = Time to recoup investment
  • IRR = Discount rate where NPV = 0
  • Used in: KA1, KA4, KA5, KA6

Survey or Questionnaire (Technique 45)

  • Purpose: Gather input from many people at scale
  • Elicitation type: Collaborative (despite being asynchronous)
  • Best for: Large, geographically dispersed stakeholder groups
  • Exam trap: Surveys ARE Collaborative in BABOK — they involve stakeholder input

Focus Groups (Technique 21)

  • Purpose: Gather reactions, attitudes, and preferences from a representative group
  • Key difference from Workshops: Focus Groups GATHER feedback; Workshops PRODUCE deliverables
  • Risk: Groupthink — dominant participants influence others
  • Elicitation type: Collaborative

4. Tier 3 — Moderately Tested Techniques

Interface Analysis (Technique 24)

  • Purpose: Examine system integration points — data formats, protocols, error handling
  • Elicitation type: Research
  • Exam tip: When the scenario involves system-to-system communication, Interface Analysis is the answer

Data Flow Diagrams (Technique 13)

  • Purpose: Show data flowing between external entities, processes, and data stores
  • Model category: Data and Information
  • Exam tip: DFDs show data MOVEMENT; ERDs show data STRUCTURE

Entity-Relationship Diagrams (part of Data Modelling — Technique 15)

  • Purpose: Model entities, attributes, and relationships
  • Model category: Data and Information
  • Exam tip: ERDs show STRUCTURE; DFDs show FLOW

State Modelling (Technique 44)

  • Purpose: Model valid states and transitions of an entity
  • Exam tip: When an entity goes through lifecycle stages (Draft → Submitted → Approved → Closed), use a State Diagram

Sequence Diagrams (Technique 42)

  • Purpose: Show message exchanges between objects/systems over time
  • Model category: Activity Flow
  • Exam tip: When the scenario describes message passing between systems in order, use Sequence Diagrams

Process Modelling (Technique 35)

  • Purpose: Create visual process flow diagrams (BPMN, flowcharts, swimlanes)
  • Model category: Activity Flow
  • Exam tip: When the scenario describes step-by-step workflow with decisions, use Process Modelling

Functional Decomposition (Technique 22)

  • Purpose: Break down a system into sub-functions hierarchically
  • Model category: Capability
  • Exam tip: When breaking a system into "modules" or "sub-functions," it's Functional Decomposition

Estimation (Technique 19)

  • Purpose: Estimate effort, time, cost for activities
  • Common methods: Analogous, Parametric, Bottom-up, Three-point (PERT)
  • Used in: KA1 (plan approach), KA2 (prepare for elicitation), KA5 (design options)

Collaborative Games (Technique 10)

  • Purpose: Creative exercises to break down barriers and uncover hidden assumptions
  • Examples: Product Box, Buy a Feature, Speedboat
  • Elicitation type: Collaborative
  • Exam tip: When stakeholders are reluctant or traditional methods aren't working, Collaborative Games engage them creatively

Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria (Technique 1)

  • Purpose: Define measurable criteria for accepting deliverables or evaluating solutions
  • Used in: KA5 (specify, validate, recommend), KA6 (measure performance)
  • Exam tip: These criteria link KA5 (defining them) to KA6 (using them for evaluation)

5. Tier 4 — Lightly Tested but Know the Purpose

CBAP Cheat Sheet — Chapter 11: Perspectives

Exam Weight: ~5-8% of questions. Perspectives are lightly tested but tricky — the exam embeds perspective-specific nuances within KA scenario questions. Know the key characteristics and how BA work adapts for each.

Perspectives describe different contexts in which business analysis is performed. They are NOT methodologies — they are LENSES that shape how BA tasks are applied.

1. Overview — The 5 Perspectives

#PerspectiveFocusKey Question It Answers
1AgileIterative, adaptive deliveryHow does BA work in short cycles with evolving requirements?
2Business IntelligenceData-driven decision makingHow does BA work when the focus is analytics, reporting, and data?
3Information TechnologySoftware/systems developmentHow does BA work within IT projects and system implementations?
4Business ArchitectureEnterprise-level strategic alignmentHow does BA work at the enterprise level across initiatives?
5Business Process ManagementProcess optimization and transformationHow does BA work when the focus is improving business processes?

Mnemonic: A-BI-IT-BA-BPM ("All Business Intelligence Is Terribly Beautiful, Please Manage")

2. Perspective 1 — Agile

Key Characteristics:

  • Iterative and incremental delivery in short cycles (sprints/iterations)
  • Requirements evolve continuously — no big upfront specification
  • Collaboration over documentation — working software over comprehensive docs
  • Continuous feedback through demos, reviews, and retrospectives
  • Self-organizing teams with embedded BA/product owner roles

How BA Work Adapts:

KAAgile Adaptation
KA1 (Planning)Lightweight planning; rolling wave; approach evolves per iteration
KA2 (Elicitation)Continuous — embedded in backlog grooming, sprint planning, daily standups
KA3 (RLCM)Product backlog replaces baseline; continuous reprioritization; PO accepts stories
KA4 (Strategy)Product vision replaces detailed future state; lean canvas; validated learning
KA5 (RADD)User stories + acceptance criteria replace formal BRDs; just-in-time elaboration
KA6 (Evaluation)Per-iteration evaluation in sprint reviews; continuous feedback loops

Key Agile Concepts for the Exam:

  • Product Owner — owns the backlog, makes prioritization decisions (equivalent of sponsor + domain SME)
  • User Stories — "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]" + acceptance criteria
  • Definition of Ready — criteria for a story to enter a sprint
  • Definition of Done — criteria for a story to be considered complete
  • Backlog Grooming/Refinement — ongoing maintenance and elaboration of backlog items
  • Velocity — team's capacity measured in story points per sprint
  • Retrospective — continuous improvement (maps to KA1 Task 5 and KA6)
  • Minimum Viable Product (MVP) — smallest product that delivers value and enables learning

Exam Traps:

  • Agile does NOT mean "no planning" — it means ADAPTIVE planning
  • Agile does NOT mean "no documentation" — it means RIGHT-SIZED documentation
  • Requirements still need confirmation, verification, and validation — just lighter-weight
  • The BA role may be filled by the Product Owner, a dedicated BA, or shared among team members

3. Perspective 2 — Business Intelligence (BI)

Key Characteristics:

  • Focus on data-driven decision making — analytics, reporting, dashboards
  • Involves data warehousing, ETL, data lakes, and analytical tools
  • Requirements center on what data, from where, transformed how, presented to whom
  • Heavy emphasis on data quality, data governance, and metadata management

How BA Work Adapts:

KABI Adaptation
KA1 (Planning)Plan for data-centric analysis; identify data sources, data stewards
KA2 (Elicitation)Elicit reporting needs, KPIs, data sources; heavy use of Document Analysis and Data Mining
KA3 (RLCM)Trace from business questions → data requirements → data sources → reports
KA4 (Strategy)Assess data maturity; define analytics roadmap; identify data gaps
KA5 (RADD)Data models, ETL specifications, report specifications, dashboard wireframes
KA6 (Evaluation)Evaluate data quality, report accuracy, analytics adoption, decision-making improvement

Key BI Concepts for the Exam:

  • Data Warehouse — centralized repository of integrated data from multiple sources
  • ETL (Extract-Transform-Load) — process for moving data from sources to warehouse
  • OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) — multi-dimensional data analysis
  • Data Quality Dimensions — accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness
  • Metadata — data about data (definitions, lineage, business rules)
  • Data Governance — policies and standards for data management
  • Self-Service BI — enabling business users to create their own reports/analytics

Key Techniques Emphasized:

  • Data Modelling, Data Dictionary, Data Flow Diagrams, Data Mining, Interface Analysis

Exam Traps:

  • BI requirements are NOT just "build me a report" — they start with BUSINESS QUESTIONS that need answers
  • Data quality issues are often the biggest risk in BI projects
  • The BA must understand both the business need and the data landscape

4. Perspective 3 — Information Technology (IT)

Key Characteristics:

  • Focus on software development, system implementation, and technology solutions
  • The MOST common context for BA work — most CBAP candidates work in this perspective
  • Requirements span functional, non-functional, and technical specifications
  • Involves SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) — whether waterfall, agile, or hybrid

How BA Work Adapts:

KAIT Adaptation
KA1 (Planning)Align BA approach with SDLC methodology; plan for technical stakeholders
KA2 (Elicitation)Elicit from business AND technical stakeholders; use prototyping, interface analysis
KA3 (RLCM)Formal traceability from business → stakeholder → solution → test; change control
KA4 (Strategy)Evaluate technology options (build/buy/configure); assess technical feasibility
KA5 (RADD)Full range of models: use cases, data models, process flows, non-functional specs, APIs
KA6 (Evaluation)Evaluate system performance, user adoption, defect rates, technical debt

Key IT Concepts for the Exam:

  • Functional Requirements — what the system DOES
  • Non-Functional Requirements — how well the system PERFORMS (quality attributes)
  • Solution Architecture — how technology components are organized
  • APIs and Integration — how systems communicate
  • Technical Debt — shortcuts taken during development that increase future maintenance costs
  • DevOps — combining development and operations for continuous delivery
  • Cloud Computing — SaaS, PaaS, IaaS delivery models

Key Techniques Emphasized:

  • Use Cases, User Stories, Data Modelling, Process Modelling, Prototyping, Interface Analysis, Non-Functional Requirements Analysis

Exam Traps:

  • The BA is NOT a developer — the BA bridges business and technical worlds
  • The BA should understand technology enough to assess feasibility but doesn't make technology decisions
  • Non-functional requirements are equally important as functional requirements

5. Perspective 4 — Business Architecture

Key Characteristics:

  • Focus on enterprise-level strategic alignment — how the organization operates as a whole
  • Operates at a HIGHER level of abstraction than individual projects
  • Concerned with business capabilities, value streams, organizational structure, and strategic alignment
  • Bridges the gap between corporate strategy and execution

How BA Work Adapts:

KABusiness Architecture Adaptation
KA1 (Planning)Enterprise-level planning; cross-initiative coordination; long-term roadmaps
KA2 (Elicitation)Elicit from executives and strategists; focus on capabilities and value streams
KA3 (RLCM)Manage enterprise-level requirements that span multiple initiatives
KA4 (Strategy)Core focus — enterprise strategy, capability assessment, value stream mapping
KA5 (RADD)Capability models, value stream maps, business motivation models, enterprise data models
KA6 (Evaluation)Evaluate whether initiatives collectively deliver on strategic objectives

Key Business Architecture Concepts for the Exam:

  • Business Capability — what the organization can do (independent of how it's done)
  • Value Stream — end-to-end set of activities that deliver value to a customer
  • Business Motivation Model — why the organization does what it does (vision, goals, strategies, tactics)
  • Enterprise Architecture Frameworks — TOGAF, Zachman (know they exist, not details)
  • Strategic Alignment — ensuring initiatives support enterprise strategy
  • Capability Mapping — assessing current vs. required capabilities

Key Techniques Emphasized:

  • Business Capability Analysis, Scope Modelling, Organizational Modelling, Business Model Canvas, SWOT Analysis, Balanced Scorecard

Exam Traps:

  • Business Architecture operates at the ENTERPRISE level — not individual project level
  • The BA in this perspective focuses on WHAT the organization needs, not HOW to build it
  • Value Streams are about CUSTOMER VALUE delivery — not internal processes alone

6. Perspective 5 — Business Process Management (BPM)

Key Characteristics:

  • Focus on understanding, improving, and transforming business processes
  • Involves the full process lifecycle — design, model, execute, monitor, optimize
  • Uses process modelling notations like BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation)
  • Emphasizes continuous process improvement — not just one-time projects

How BA Work Adapts:

KABPM Adaptation
KA1 (Planning)Plan for process-centric analysis; identify process owners and stakeholders
KA2 (Elicitation)Elicit current processes using observation, process analysis, workshops
KA3 (RLCM)Trace from business goals → process requirements → process designs → implementations
KA4 (Strategy)Assess process maturity; identify process improvement opportunities; define process goals
KA5 (RADD)As-is and to-be process models; process performance metrics; automation opportunities
KA6 (Evaluation)Measure process performance (cycle time, cost, quality); continuous monitoring

Key BPM Concepts for the Exam:

  • BPMN — standard notation for process modelling (pools, lanes, gateways, events, tasks)
  • Process Lifecycle — Design → Model → Execute → Monitor → Optimize (continuous cycle)
  • As-Is vs. To-Be — current state process vs. future state process
  • Process Owner — the person accountable for a process's performance
  • Process Maturity — how well-defined and managed processes are (CMM levels)
  • Automation — using technology to automate manual process steps (RPA, workflow engines)
  • Continuous Improvement — Lean, Six Sigma, Kaizen — ongoing process optimization
  • Key Process Metrics — cycle time, throughput, error rate, cost per transaction

Key Techniques Emphasized:

  • Process Modelling, Process Analysis, Observation, Benchmarking, Metrics and KPIs, Root Cause Analysis

Exam Traps:

  • BPM is CONTINUOUS — not a one-time project. The monitor-optimize cycle never ends
  • Process improvement doesn't always require technology — sometimes it's about removing steps or reassigning work
  • The BA in BPM must understand both the process and the organizational context

7. Cross-Perspective Comparison Table

DimensionAgileBIITBusiness ArchitectureBPM
Primary FocusIterative deliveryData & analyticsSystems & softwareEnterprise strategyProcess optimization
Abstraction LevelTeam/projectData layerSystem/projectEnterpriseProcess/organization
Requirements FormatUser storiesData/report specsUse cases, specsCapability modelsProcess models
Key StakeholdersProduct Owner, Dev TeamData stewards, analystsBusiness & IT usersExecutives, strategistsProcess owners, operators
Change ApproachIncremental iterationsData maturity roadmapSDLC (various)Strategic roadmapContinuous improvement
Key ModelsStory maps, backlogsData models, ETL specsUML, ERDs, DFDsValue streams, capabilitiesBPMN, swimlanes
Evaluation FocusSprint reviews, velocityData quality, adoptionSystem performance, defectsStrategic alignmentProcess metrics

8. How Perspectives Relate to Knowledge Areas

All 5 perspectives use ALL 6 knowledge areas — but each perspective EMPHASIZES different aspects:

PerspectiveHeaviest KA Emphasis
AgileKA2 (continuous elicitation), KA3 (backlog management)
BIKA5 (data modelling), KA2 (data source elicitation)
ITKA5 (full specification), KA3 (formal traceability)
Business ArchitectureKA4 (strategy), KA5 (capability modelling)
BPMKA4 (process strategy), KA5 (process modelling), KA6 (process evaluation)

9. Key Exam Points — What Gets Tested

  • "Which perspective is this scenario describing?" — identify the perspective from context clues
  • "How does BA work adapt in [perspective]?" — know the KA adaptations
  • Agile is the MOST tested perspective — by far the heaviest exam weight among the five
  • Perspectives are LENSES, not methodologies — they shape how BA work is done, not replace it
  • All KAs apply in ALL perspectives — perspectives change HOW tasks are done, not WHETHER they're done
  • Common trap: "KA3 doesn't apply in Agile" — FALSE. RLCM applies through backlog management
  • Common trap: "KA4 doesn't apply in BPM" — FALSE. Strategy analysis assesses process maturity and goals
  • The BA role may look different across perspectives — Product Owner in Agile, Data Analyst in BI, Process Analyst in BPM — but the core BA skills remain the same

10. Quick-Fire Summary

  • 5 perspectives: Agile, BI, IT, Business Architecture, BPM
  • Perspectives are LENSES, not methodologies — they shape how BA work is performed
  • ALL 6 KAs apply in ALL perspectives — the tasks adapt, they don't disappear
  • Agile = iterative, user stories, backlog, continuous feedback, PO role
  • BI = data-driven, ETL, data quality, reports/dashboards, analytics
  • IT = systems development, functional + non-functional requirements, SDLC
  • Business Architecture = enterprise strategy, capabilities, value streams, strategic alignment
  • BPM = process optimization, BPMN, as-is/to-be, continuous improvement, process metrics
  • Agile is the most tested perspective on the CBAP exam
  • Know how EACH KA adapts for EACH perspective — especially Agile
